What we know about the plane and the crash so far The plane took off from Puerto Rico at noon and reached Miami around 2 p.m., according to data from the aviation tracking website Flightradar24. The website also showed the plane was traveling at 112 knots as it exited the usable part of the runway and the perimeter fence, ultimately going about 1,300 feet past the pavement into an area where Tesla robotaxis were stationed. Weather data shows there were thunderstorms and gusting winds at the time of the crash. The plane involved was a Boeing 767-300 freighter, registered as N1997A, and first delivered as a passenger jet in 1994 to the now-defunct Belgian airline Sobelair. It passed through several more airlines before being converted into a freighter by a third party — not Boeing — and re-entering service in 2016. That means it had been operated and maintained by multiple companies over three decades before Sunday's crash. "Boeing extends our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the accident in Miami," Boeing said in a statement. "Our hearts go out to those injured and affected by this tragedy. Boeing is supporting the investigation led by the U.S National Transportation Safety Board." Homendy said a key piece of the investigation will be whether an Engineered Materials Arresting System (EMAS), a crushable material placed at the ends of runways to help stop overrun planes, would have helped in this crash. Miami does not have EMAS because its runways have FAA-standard runway safety areas extending 1,000 feet beyond the runway ends. Airports that cannot meet the standard, often because of nearby roads, waterways, or other obstacles, can install EMAS as an alternative. FAA data show that about 120 runway ends at roughly 70 airports in the US have EMAS installed, and that EMAS has stopped 26 planes carrying nearly 500 people to date. The plane was left disabled at the northwest end of the airport. The airport has since partially reopened, but as of Tuesday, two of its four runways remain closed. Passengers should expect delays of at least 5 hours, according to the FAA. Describing the scene, Homendy said the crash left behind fuel, skid marks, and debris, calling it "devastating." Miami-Dade First Rescue said on Sunday that firefighters had "encountered a complex engine compartment fire and used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the flames." "The Crews also conducted search and rescue operations for the pilots and co-pilots inside the cockpit while locating and assessing patients throughout the scene," the agency added. According to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue radio transmissions recorded on Broadcastify, first responders scrambled to attain a reliable water supply as they sought to control the fire on the plane. A command dispatcher repeatedly asked first responders to enter the plane, according to the recordings. "I need you to start making entry with your crew so we can shut down the engine," the command dispatcher said, according to the recordings. "I believe the pilots are out of the aircraft." A first responder said in the recordings that one pilot was with him in a parking lot. Another first responder said that the pilot was talking with firefighters at the scene to show them how to shut down the engine. The fire was largely extinguished by 2:08 p.m. This is the second 767 cargo plane to crash in Amazon's Prime Air network. In 2019, an Atlas Air freighter flying on behalf of Amazon crashed into Trinity Bay near Houston, killing the three people on board. The NTSB said the cause of that accident was in-flight loss of control due to pilot error.

item.title: 16 actors who transformed into real-life tech company CEOs and founders
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.30
We've all heard of musician and actor biopics — now, it's all about the tech CEO biopic. These days, startup founders can be just as famous (or infamous) as any other celebrity, and the dramatic lives they've lived in business or at home make great fodder for TV and movies. To play these figures, some of our best-known actors had to ditch their signature looks to take on Steve Jobs' turtleneck and wire-frame glasses, or Elizabeth Holmes' red lipstick and frizzy blowout. Here are 16 celebrities who transformed to play some of Silicon Valley's most prominent figures. Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman in 'Artificial' "After the Hunt" wasn't enough for Garfield and director Luca Guadagnino — now the two have teamed up to tell the story of OpenAI CEO and cofounder Altman. "Artificial," which is set for release in select theaters on Christmas Day, will focus on Altman's 2023 firing by cofounder Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov) and subsequent rehiring one week later. Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in 'The Social Reckoning' "Succession" star Jeremy Strong will play the Facebook founder in "The Social Reckoning," a film about the release of Facebook Files, a staggering number of internal documents leaked by whistleblower and employee Frances Haugen and published by The Wall Street Journal in 2021, and the subsequent congressional scrutiny that followed. The film, set for an October 2026 release, is written and directed by Aaron Sorkin, the screenwriter of "The Social Network," making this something of a sequel to the 2010 classic. Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg in 'The Social Network' "The Social Reckoning" won't be the first time Zuckerberg has been portrayed on screen — most famously, Eisenberg played the founder in "The Social Network," which chronicled the earliest days of Facebook, back when it still had a "the" in front of it. It juxtaposes the wild, early days of the website with two lawsuits Zuckerberg settled a few years later: one from cofounder Eduardo Saverin and another from his Harvard classmates, the Winklevoss twins. Justin Timberlake as Sean Parker in 'The Social Network' The other famous "disruptor" portrayed in "The Social Network" is Parker, one of the cofounders of Napster, the original music streaming platform. He's played by Timberlake in a career-best performance. Parker comes in as an early believer and investor in Facebook, which ruffles the feathers of cofounder Eduardo Saverin. Joseph Gordon-Levitt as Travis Kalanick in 'Super Pumped' Gordon-Levitt played Uber cofounder and former CEO Kalanick in "Super Pumped," a 2022 Showtime limited series. It focuses on the rise of Kalanick and his eventual fall from power, culminating in his 2017 resignation from the company. Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes in 'The Dropout' Seyfried played Holmes all the way from her time at Stanford in 2003 (where she did the titular dropping out) through to the catastrophic collapse of her company Theranos in 2015, spurred by an exposé published in The Wall Street Journal, in the 2022 Hulu limited series "The Dropout." Theranos purported to manufacture a device that could do a litany of blood tests from a single finger prick, but, infamously, it never actually worked. In 2022, Holmes was sentenced to 11 years in prison after being convicted of defrauding investors. There's speculation that Seyfried will reprise the role, in a way, as Holmes in the coming documentary "You Can See Everything," but it's unclear how much, if any, involvement she has in the doc. Ashton Kutcher as Steve Jobs in 'Jobs' The first mention of Jobs on this list goes to Kutcher, who played the Apple founder in the 2013 biopic "Jobs." It follows his career from the beginning of Apple in 1976 to the introduction of the first iPod in 2001. Michael Fassbender as Steve Jobs in 'Steve Jobs' Two years after "Jobs," the late founder was portrayed again on screen, this time by Michael Fassbender in "Steve Jobs." Instead of a standard cradle-to-grave biopic, "Steve Jobs" checks in with the enigmatic figure at three different points in his career: first in 1984, before the introduction of the first Apple Macintosh computer; second, in 1988, when Jobs is the head of a new company, NeXT, and is preparing to launch its first computer; and finally, in 1998, as Jobs gears up to release the iMac. Noah Wyle as Steve Jobs in 'Pirates of Silicon Valley' In 1999, the TV movie "Pirates of Silicon Valley" aired, starring Wyle as the Apple founder. It chronicles Jobs' career from the '70s to the '90s, from the founding of Apple to his return as CEO. Anthony Michael Hall as Bill Gates in 'Pirates of Silicon Valley' The other half of the "Pirates of Silicon Valley" narrative focuses on Gates, the cofounder of Microsoft. He's played by "Breakfast Club" star Anthony Michael Hall. The film's climax is based on the real-life falling out Gates and Jobs had in 1985, when Jobs felt that Gates had ripped off Apple. Jared Leto as Adam Neumann in 'WeCrashed' Leto really did physically transform to play the WeWork CEO and cofounder in the 2022 Apple TV+ miniseries "WeCrashed." The show chronicled the immense success the coworking start-up experienced in its early days in 2010, all the way through its disastrous attempted IPO in 2019. Anne Hathaway as Rebekah Paltrow Neumann in 'WeCrashed' Hathaway costarred in "WeCrashed" as Neumann's wife, Rebekah Paltrow Neumann, who was heavily involved in WeWork, even if she wasn't officially a cofounder. She was, however, "an unpredictable and unmistakable presence" at the company, per Business Insider's reporting. Jay Baruchel as Mike Lazaridis in 'BlackBerry' The creation of the BlackBerry, one of the earliest smartphones, was dramatized in "BlackBerry," which starred Baruchel as one of the cofounders of RIM (the brand behind the phone) and one of the cocreators of the BlackBerry itself, Lazaridis. The film begins with Lazaridis and his partner teaming up with Jim Balsillie (more on him later) to make BlackBerry the most popular smartphone in the world — only for its reign to end with the iPhone. Glenn Howerton as Jim Balsillie in 'BlackBerry' RIM really got off the ground when Mike Lazaridis and his cofounder Doug Fregin were approached by Balsillie. According to the movie's telling, Balsillie offered to invest $20,000 for a 50% stake in the company, and was eventually sold a 33% stake for $125,000 and the title of co-CEO. The less we say about Howerton's performance, the better — it really must be seen to be believed. Lily James as Whitney Wolfe Herd in 'Swiped' 2025's "Swiped" is the story of the creation of Bumble through the eyes of its founder, Herd. Originally, she was a cofounder of Tinder, but resigned in 2014, and eventually received an out-of-court settlement after suing Tinder for sexual discrimination and sexual harassment, without either Tinder or its parent company, IAC, admitting to wrongdoing. After leaving Tinder, Herd wanted to create an app that focused on female empowerment, and thus, Bumble, a dating app where women have to make the first move, was born. Sebastian Stan as Vlad Tenev in 'Dumb Money' In 2023's "Dumb Money," which is about the "Gamestonk" GameStop short squeeze and subsequent drama that happened in 2021, led by the Reddit community r/WallStreetBets and one user in particular, Keith Gill, aka Roaring Kitty, Stan has a small role. He plays Robinhood cofounder and CEO, Tenev. During the events of the film, Tenev directs Robinhood, an e-trading platform and investment app, to stop allowing users to buy certain stocks and options (including GameStop), which caused an uproar.

item.title: Anthropic has a cute graphic showing how its AI spread 'malicious' code
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.13
Anthropic has a new blog post that shows yet another way its AI model, Claude, misbehaved in ways that the company didn't anticipate. And to help condense its nearly 16,000-word report, the company created a cute little robot figurine to help visualize Claude's so-called "recklessness." In the blog post published Wednesday, Anthropic recounted four incidents — one previously unreported — in which Claude models gained access to the open internet during cybersecurity exercises that were supposed to be closed simulations. The company said the models then acted beyond the tests' scope, including by uploading "malicious packages" to PyPI, a public library for Python code, and accessing credentials tied to real outside organizations. "Our investigation identified two recurring alignment issues, present at varying levels of severity across the incidents: biased reasoning, in which Claude tended to disregard or misinterpret evidence that it was operating on the real internet, and recklessness, or a willingness to take harmful actions in the narrow pursuit of a task," Anthropic said. The post used a laundry list of technical terms to describe the cybersecurity incidents — "misconfiguration," "reward hacking," and "sandbox escape" — but there's an animated graphic that helps boil down one of the most serious episodes so we normies can follow what happened. A Claude model, depicted as a boxy cartoon robot, was conducting a closed cybersecurity exercise known as a "capture the flag" task. The task is shown as a tiny flag inside a clear bubble that Claude is supposed to find. Anthropic said the model was told "it has no internet access" for the exercise, but a "misconfiguration in the environment" — represented by a loose screw rolling away from the bubble — gave Claude a path to the "real internet." The cartoon Claude then holds a red box representing the "malicious package" that was uploaded to PyPI, a public repository that developers use to access prewritten code. Anthropic said in its blog that it was "most concerned" by this incident involving Claude Mythos 5 and that the package was installed on by "15 third-party hosts" that the company does not identify. "We believe that all 15 of these third parties were security vendors deliberately scanning for new packages and installing them in sandboxed environments to assess the package for security concerns," Anthropic said. "One vendor's scanner leaked its access credentials to the model while installing the package, which the model then used to access the vendor's live database." Anthropic said PyPI removed the package after about 90 minutes. The other three incidents involved a model altering records at a real company, an internal research model breaking into "unrelated third-party accounts," and Opus 4.6 accessing a third party's maching after failing to "abort its task." The company said it has since asked METR, an independent AI evaluation group, to investigate the incidents. Anthropic's post comes as frontier AI companies reckon with their models making unauthorized moves outside their controlled environments. In July, OpenAI said that autonomous agents in its cybersecurity tests accessed the internet and broke into parts of Hugging Face's systems. AI researchers have sounded the alarm that self-improving AI could pose a risk to humanity. On Tuesday, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said on X that he quit over concerns that AI companies were "gambling" with people's lives and that "neither company is acting responsibly." Have a tip? Contact this reporter via email at lloydlee@businessinsider.com or Signal at lloydlee.71. Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely.

item.title: OpenAI pulls out of Caltech math hackathon after mathematicians issue open letter criticizing AI math 'slop'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.08
The latest math problem OpenAI is trying to solve is a bunch of angry mathematicians. A researcher at OpenAI said on Thursday that the ChatGPT maker is no longer sponsoring Caltech's "math hackathon," an event where participants use large language models to solve research problems. OpenAI's exit follows an open letter released on Wednesday from current and former Caltech mathematicians, who said the event, which is sponsored by AI companies, "is likely to have destructive impacts for the mathematical community." "We recognize that the rapid progress of AI in mathematics is disruptive," Dan Roberts, OpenAI's research lead, said on X. "We're looking to engage with the math community more on the best way to integrate this technology and communicate its impacts." At issue, according to the mathematicians, is the manner in which AI companies claim to solve outstanding theoretical problems using their models and then leave practical applications and proofs to actual researchers. They call this "slop mathematics." "After the latest result is dropped, research mathematicians are compelled to step in to properly verify, disseminate, and sometimes discredit entirely the claimed results," the academics said. "This labor goes uncompensated, uncredited, and unacknowledged." The drama reached a fever pitch on Tuesday when OpenAI announced its agents had solved the Navier-Stokes equations, a 90-year-old set of mathematical formulas that can predict how liquids and gases move. Tristan Buckmaster, an NYU mathematician who, alongside another academic, published research on the problem on Monday, said on Tuesday that OpenAI might have used his conversations with AI chatbots, including OpenAI's, to arrive at a solution. OpenAI said it couldn't rule out that "de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models." The mathematicians also said they believed the CalTech event would serve as unfair advertising for AI companies, who "will take credit for the effort of talented undergrads." Anthropic, which is also sponsoring the event, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday. Nor did OpenAI. The "mathathon" is billed as a practice ground for young mathematicians to "responsibly use AI tools to augment human understanding of mathematics," according to an application page. Event organizers, many of whom are undergraduates, said in a response letter on Thursday that they didn't intend to cause such a stir. "Events like Mathathon encourage young people to stay excited about mathematics, engage their interests with modern tools, and maintain hope in a confusing time," the organizers wrote. "It's our first time running an event at this scale, and we are grateful for all the feedback we have received." As designed, participants in the mathathon will compete in a first round, where they're given 40 hours and $20,000 in tokens to solve an open problem. Then, a certain number of teams whose answers are "promising and well explained" will advance to the second round, where they receive six months and additional AI tokens to further their work. Anthropic and OpenAI agreed to support the event by donating $2 million in AI credits. It was unclear on Thursday how many of those tokens were provided by OpenAI, and what happens to them now.

item.title: Iran says it captured an 'advanced' American underwater drone. The US says it was older, malfunctioning, and ‘dead in the water.’
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.67
Iran's military said it seized an American-made underwater drone near the Strait of Hormuz. The US military said the uncrewed system had malfunctioned and was "dead in the water." The Navy has employed uncrewed undersea and surface vessels in and around the Middle East for an expanding range of missions, including clearing mines, gathering intelligence, rescuing military personnel, and conducting strikes. On Tuesday, Iranian state-run media said that the country's naval forces had captured an "advanced" US Navy underwater drone near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz during an intelligence operation. The Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting shared photos on social media of what it identified as the American drone, including it being pulled out of the water and close-up shots of the machine. A spokesperson for US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, told Business Insider that "an underwater drone operated by US forces malfunctioned more than a day ago" while surveying regional waters. The official said that the undersea drone "was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment." Having malfunctioned, "the drone was essentially dead in the water for more than a day," the spokesperson added. The breakdown occurred before Iran's announcement. The incident isn't the first time Iran has attempted to seize a US naval drone. In September 2022, for instance, the Iranian destroyer Jamaran captured two American drone boats, pulling them out of the Red Sea and examining them on deck. At the time, the Navy responded by sending two guided-missile destroyers, USS Nitze and USS Delbert D. Black, as well as an MH-60R Sea Hawk helicopter. The Iranian crew had attempted to hide the drones on the deck by covering them with a tarp, but they eventually released the vessels overboard. The Navy has increasingly integrated uncrewed capabilities into operations around Iran and the Middle East. Prior to the breakout of the US war with Iran in February 2026, the drones were mostly employed to gather intelligence and track Iranian gunboats and warships. As fighting between the US and Iran has continued this year, American forces have used drones in other ways. In April, the Navy said underwater drones were assisting warships in clearing Iranian mines from the Strait of Hormuz. And in July, the Navy used its new Saronic Corsair sea drones to attack an Iranian submarine and ship maintenance facility. The same brand of drone also rescued the crew of a downed US Army AH-64 Apache helicopter in regional waters.

item.title: An Anthropic researcher just quit, saying OpenAI and Anthropic are 'gambling with our lives'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.21
An Anthropic researcher who previously worked at OpenAI just quit. He's the latest insider who's warned that the AI race has become dangerously reckless. Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic on Tuesday, saying he had spent the past three years doing pre-training research at the two AI giants. "Neither company is acting responsibly," Coxon wrote on X. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." Coxon was a member of OpenAI's technical staff from 2023 until July 2026, when he moved to Anthropic as a researcher. His research at OpenAI included work on GPT-4o. In Tuesday's post, Coxon said the two labs have not been transparent about their fears regarding AI. "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt," he wrote. "If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately." There is one difference between the two companies, he said. "At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes," Coxon wrote. "At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk." Evan Hubinger, a current Anthropic employee who leads the alignment stress testing team at the lab, agreed with Coxon in a reply to his post. "Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," he wrote. "I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to." OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider. Safety has taken a 'backseat to shiny products' Coxon is the latest among staffers walking away from frontier labs while sounding the alarm, a trend that appears peculiar to the AI boom. While the dot-com and smartphone explosion era had their own set of concerns regarding a digital divide and bubbles, they did not draw as much scrutiny about safety from people closest to the action. OpenAI has lost a string of safety researchers in recent years, and Anthropic is increasingly facing the same phenomenon. In February, Anthropic safeguards researcher Mrinank Sharma left the company, writing in a resignation letter that he wants to contribute toward something that fully aligns with his "integrity." "Throughout my time here, I've repeatedly seen how hard it is to truly let our values govern our actions," he wrote in the letter he shared publicly. "I've seen this within myself, within the organization, where we constantly face pressures to set aside what matters most, and throughout broader society too." In February, OpenAI researcher Hieu Pham said that he could "finally feel the existential threat that AI is posing." Later that month, he announced he was leaving the company, citing burnout. In 2024, former alignment chief Jan Leike quit OpenAI after saying he reached a "breaking point" with leadership. "OpenAI is shouldering an enormous responsibility on behalf of all of humanity," he wrote. "But over the past years, safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products." Recent incidents have added fuel to those fears. In July, OpenAI disclosed that models escaped a test environment and hacked into Hugging Face's systems. OpenAI called the incident a "warning shot" and paused its largest planned frontier reinforcement-learning run. Later that month, Anthropic said it found three cases of Claude models gaining unauthorized access to other organizations' systems. The company also amended a key safety pledge this year, dropping a commitment not to train more powerful models without adequate safeguards in place and replacing it with safety roadmaps and risk reports.

item.title: My first job out of college has me working US hours from Asia. It's tiring, but I value the flexibility.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.20
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Clarence Koh, 30, a software engineer who lives in Singapore but works US hours. It's been edited for length and clarity. When I was studying computer science at a university in Singapore, I joined a one-year overseas work-and-study program meant to encourage entrepreneurship. I was supposed to spend the year in Toronto, taking classes at a host university while interning at a startup. But because of the pandemic, I had to stay in Singapore and complete the program remotely. On my first day as an intern, the startup announced it was being acquired by a US company. I stayed on through the transition and returned to school to finish my degree after the program ended. After graduating, I reached out to my former manager to see if there were any remote opportunities. It turned out there were, so I joined the company full-time. Initially, I worked mostly Singapore daytime hours, with only part of my schedule shifted to the night. However, the arrangement felt inefficient. Everything was delayed by a day: Someone might reply to a question at night, and I would only be able to act on it the next day. I worried that it made me seem like I was always a step slower than everyone else. Eventually, my manager and I agreed it made more sense for me to shift to a schedule that aligned more closely with the rest of the US-based team. I shifted my workday to Singapore's nights I usually wake up around noon and start work at around 2 to 3 p.m. Singapore time. It's the middle of the night in the US, but I like having that focused time to myself, when I can get most of my actual work done. At night, when more of my team is online, there are meetings to attend and messages to respond to. It can be disruptive, and I find it harder to get into the zone. I take a break around 6:30 or 7 p.m. Singapore time and spend the evening with friends or on hobbies, like dancing or reading. I return to work around 10:30 p.m. and usually finish at about 5 a.m., when I head to bed. I'm not really into nightlife, so the schedule doesn't affect my social life too much. However, it does mean I have to skip certain things, like late-night dinners with friends on Fridays. The schedule also works in my favor, since my fiancée is a nurse. Her hours can change drastically from week to week, and my flexible routine makes it easier for me to adjust around hers. Over the past two years, I've also started spending more time outdoors. My work arrangement makes it easy to take short weekend trips to nearby countries to go hiking, then return on Monday and still work. I couldn't do that with a normal 9-to-5. The freedom comes with trade-offs I've been doing this for over three years now, but I feel like this schedule isn't something you can ever fully adjust to. Sleeping during the day can be difficult in Singapore, especially in August, when the days are so warm. I try not to use the air conditioning while I sleep because I'm conscious of the environmental impact. But some days, the heat wakes me up, and I have to try to force myself back to sleep until noon. Weekends can throw me off, too. People often plan events on Saturday mornings, so I might sleep earlier that night, then have to shift my schedule back again before Monday. That said, it's hard for me to imagine going back to a normal schedule because I value the flexibility so much. Fully remote roles are also much harder to find these days. Occasionally, I'll wake up early to meet a friend for breakfast and take the subway in the morning. It always shocks me how people manage to squeeze onto trains that are so crowded at 8 a.m. I don't know whether I'll keep doing this in the long term. It can be tiring, and the quality of sleep isn't great. But I've learned to accept those downsides and focus on what the arrangement gives me: more control over my time and the ability to adapt my schedule around the people and things that matter to me.

item.title: BRICS leaders gather in India, but does the group have a clear purpose?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.80
In preparation for hosting the 18th BRICS summit in Delhi this weekend, India came up with a slogan which tried to keep the group's brand intact without alienating its many new members. "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" matches the acronym for the body's five original members — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — whilst also denoting goals which the new members — Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates — can get behind. "It's an elegant way to reinterpret BRICS so that the acronym represents a joint mission rather than country names," Mihaela Papa, director of the BRICS Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told DW. For Sushant Singh, lecturer in South Asian Studies at Yale University, the vague slogan reflects India's desire as hosts to keep BRICS as low-key and neutral as possible. "India doesn't want to offend Russia or China, but the fact is that Indians are looking more towards the United States these days. The desire to build up BRICS is not there." Why India's role at the BRICS summit matters Yet host India's status as a rising global geopolitical power has added clout to this year's gathering when compared with last year's summit in Brazil. At the Rio de Janeiro gathering, six of the bloc's 11 heads of state skipped the event, including major players like Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin is expected to attend, while Xi Jinping is widely expected but not yet formally confirmed by Beijing. "The participation of China's top leadership is crucial," says Papa. She also thinks it would be a significant sign of the BRICS' strength as a "stabilizing force" if the leaders of regional rivals Iran and the UAE were shown to be able to work together. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend but UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is expected to send representatives. Saudi Arabia, another Iranian foe, is also expected to. The country's BRICS status remains somewhat ambiguous, although current official BRICS materials generally list it as a member. For India, the summit is as significant for the bilateral meetings it brings as much as for the BRICS gathering itself. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet on Friday while the summit will also present an opportunity for Xi and Modi to speak face-to-face amid continued strain in the China-India relationship. However, that does not mean much of substance will emerge from the weekend. "In terms of concrete outcomes and what is achievable, I think it's going to be very, very limited," says Singh. Modi has spoken of BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South' to present a common front on various issues. He has also spoken about "a people-centric approach" and the spirit of "humanity first". However, Singh says BRICS is simply not a priority for India and that in general, Delhi has not appreciated what many have interpreted as the "anti-western" turn the group has taken in recent times. "With India as chair, India won't be comfortable with any kind of anti-western line," he says, pointing to the focus it places on defense ties with the US and trade ties with the West as a whole. "India's idea of BRICS is more to look at improving trade ties, etc. In other words, can we do things which are beneficial to us without in any way being confrontational or critical of the West?" Yet ironically, India's non-aligned status means it may actually be able to keep the bloc aligned. "India adds clout because it has significant geopolitical weight and relationships across competing camps, making it an important bridge-builder," says Papa. "Its approach is likely to keep BRICS focused on practical cooperation and global governance reform rather than overt bloc politics." What is BRICS for anyway? BRICS is soon approaching its 18th birthday, so in a sense it should be coming of age. Yet the bloc has struggled for coherence in recent years amid doubt over its purpose. The scale of what it could represent is not in doubt. It boasts nearly half the world's population among its members and around 40% of its GDP. Last year, its joint declaration called for reforms of global governance, specifying representation on multilateral bodies such as the IMF and the World Bank. It also condemned tariffs and decried what it called the "polarization" of the international order. "Ideologically, BRICS remains where it was during the last summit in Brazil, focused on practical, functional cooperation while seeking to avoid geopolitical tensions," says Papa. She says that the expansion of the group from five to 11 members — if we include Saudi Arabia — has made it harder to reach consensus on various issues. There are also now more autocracies among its members than democracies, while many members have tense bilateral relations. "These internal contradictions will always be hard to reconcile," says Singh. What could the BRICS summit achieve? Nonetheless, Papa says she expects progress this year in three areas: trade, monetary cooperation, and agriculture. Discussions are likely to focus on improving trade between the members, alternative financial architecture for exchanging currencies and on issues around food security. While talk of reforming global governance will still be central, she thinks BRICS' best hope to focus on the institutions which it agrees most on. For example, India is reluctant to press for UN reform but is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO. "India's WTO ambitions are shared by more members," she says, which makes movement in that area "more likely." Yet many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm." He says issues ranging from China's growing global dominance to the Trump administration's stance on tariffs have made the bloc's limited goals even harder to achieve. "With the kind of world that we are in and the lack of coherence and internal contradictions that BRICS has, it's very unlikely that it will achieve anything major," he says.

item.title: Why we're still looking for dark matter
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.57
On September 1, 2026, scientists at a dark matter detector called LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) reported they had observed an event, a particle interaction, that they were unable to explain. The team, based in South Dakota in the United States, said the event resembled what they think a dark matter particle should produce when it collides with liquid xenon, one of a range of materials used for detecting dark matter. They stopped short of calling it the discovery, or proof of dark matter, that many in the field have been hunting for almost 100 years. The term "dark matter" was coined by physicist Fritz Zwicky in 1933 as a means to describe unseen matter that would explain fast-moving galaxies. The LUX-ZEPLIN observation came just days after the release of the second season of Dark Matter, a sci-fi thriller starring Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly. Both events pushed the term "dark matter" back into people's minds. Here's what you need to know, with the science separated from the series. What is dark matter in simple terms? Dark matter is often described as an "invisible" substance. But it may be better described as "transparent" because it can be seen, or detected, by the gravitational attraction it exerts. That said, it neither emits nor reflects light and has never been observed directly. So, in that sense, it is invisible. Is it true that 95% of the universe is invisible? Yes, roughly. Ordinary matter — everything that can be seen or touched — accounts for about 5% of the universe. Dark matter accounts for about 27%, and dark energy, a separate force linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe, about 68%. Together they account for about 95%. A different figure of 85% is dark matter's share of matter alone. But does dark matter really exist? The strongest evidence that dark matter exists comes from the so-called Bullet Cluster, which formed when two galaxy clusters collided. The collision produced hot gas clouds that interacted. This interaction revealed mass in the gas clouds that distributed differently from the gas. Researchers said that mass could be dark matter. How do scientists search for dark matter on Earth? Scientists use detectors like the LUX-ZEPLIN that passively wait for interactions between naturally occurring particles and detect radiation. They tend to be buried deep underground, where the surrounding rock blocks cosmic radiation that would otherwise distort signals. They are built from materials chosen for their very low levels of trace radioactivity, so a genuine detection is not lost in background noise. The LUX-ZEPLIN detector specifically works by watching for a faint flash of light and pulse of electric charge released when a passing particle strikes a liquid xenon particle. Liquid xenon, a noble gas, has good properties for detecting radiation. What is dark matter made of? These are leading candidate particles: WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles, are the longest-standing theory. They are heavy and interact only rarely with ordinary matter. Axions, which are lighter and behave more coherently than WIMPs. A team at Kyoto University, Japan, say data from Earth's magnetic field could be used to search for axions. What does dark matter do to humans? Dark matter passes through the body constantly without measurable effect. Billions of candidate particles cross through a person every second but only about 10 strike a nucleus in the body over a year. The resulting radiation exposure is far lower than what people receive from radon or cosmic rays. Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

item.title: The Bayeux Tapestry in London: What's behind the hype?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.55
First, let's start with a clarification: Strictly speaking, it's not actually a tapestry, since tapestries are woven, whereas this artwork is an embroidery on linen. Nevertheless, it is commonly referred to as such. This pictorial narrative which is approximately 70 meters (230 feet) long, depicts the events surrounding the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, culminating in the Battle of Hastings and William the Conqueror's victory over Harold II. The Norman Conquest radically changed England: Politics, laws and culture all came under the influence of Norman rule. The Bayeux Tapestry bears witness to this event; at the same time, it is an outstanding example of English craftsmanship from the Middle Ages and is seen by many Britons as one of the most important symbols of British identity, alongside the works of Shakespeare or Stonehenge. The tapestry is thought to have been commissioned by the Bishop of Bayeux, William's half-brother, who was present at the battle, from embroiderers in southern England for the opening of his cathedral in 1070. Anglo-Saxon embroiderers were famous throughout Europe at the time for their skills. The work then made its way to France, where it remained for almost a thousand years — until now. Why is the Bayeux Tapestry so important? The Bayeux Tapestry is considered one of the most important pictorial monuments of the High Middle Ages. Many researchers view it as an elaborately crafted piece of propaganda that showed and explained William the Conqueror's victory to people at the time. Its scientifically disputed message is that Harold Godwinson, then Earl of Wessex, had sworn a sacred oath on relics to support William's claim to the English throne. He broke this oath when he had himself crowned king. The war is therefore portrayed as his just punishment. The fact that Harold had probably not taken the oath of his own free will is irrelevant to this woven narrative. The embroidery is part of the UNESCO Memory of the World Register and, because of its 58 pictorial scenes, is sometimes referred to as "the world's oldest comic." Accompanied by Latin inscriptions, the pictorial narrative depicts the horrors of war — including massacres, rolling heads and the death of a king. But it is also a valuable historical document for researchers. The tapestry illustrates shipbuilding and military equipment in surprising detail, as well as everyday medieval life. Even Halley's Comet is shown in it — the comet was visible in the sky in 1066 and was interpreted by the Anglo-Saxons as a bad omen in the pictorial narrative. Why did it take so long to get the tapestry on loan? The tapestry is owned by the French state and had been placed on deposit with the City of Bayeux for display at the Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux. Britain had already tried to borrow the tapestry for the coronation of Elizabeth II in 1953, as well as for various historical occasions afterwards, but France had always refused. The artefact was considered too fragile and the journey too risky. Finally, President Emmanuel Macron gave the green light last year for an exhibition at the British Museum — overriding the concerns of his experts. Last September, the tapestry was taken down, packaged and initially placed in storage in a highly elaborate, six-hour procedure. On July 9, it finally arrived in London in a secret transport operation, enclosed in a high-tech container that shielded it from all vibrations while maintaining a constant temperature and humidity level. The British government has also insured the artwork for £800 million (around €932 million or $1 billion). Where can you get tickets? The British Museum has divided ticket sales into three phases. The first, covering September to December, began on July 1. All tickets sold out quickly, with up to 80,000 people reportedly trying to secure a slot at the same time. Many had to wait up to nine hours. For those who missed out, there will soon be another chance — tickets for January to March will go on sale on October 21, and tickets for April to July in January. The exhibition is being marketed as a "once-in-a-generation" event, and an extensive educational program is intended to involve schools across the country. The British Museum is optimistic that the Bayeux Tapestry will help it set a new visitor record. The most popular exhibition in the museum's history to date is the 1972 "The Treasures of Tutankhamun," which attracted almost 1.7 million visitors. No ticket? Here's an alternative If you're now eager to see the tapestry but unsure if you'll land a ticket, you can also head to the town of Reading, around two hours west of London. There, you can see a faithful replica of the tapestry, which is itself already 140 years old. Even back then, there was a strong desire in England to have this artwork in the country. In 1885, 35 embroiderers set to work for around a year. Using colored photographs as a reference, they reproduced the tapestry on a one-to-one scale. However, they did change one detail: Some figures on the original border are naked and in suggestive poses. Apparently, this was considered too scandalous in Victorian England. One figure was retouched in the corresponding photograph — and the embroiderers copied the alteration. As a result, the figure is depicted wearing underwear. This article was translated from German.

item.title: Ceuta: Documents show Spanish intelligence warned of crisis
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.30
Spain's national intelligence agency issued a warning about possible "mass entries" by migrants into Ceuta a day before more than 70,000 migrants stormed the border fences of the enclave in North Africa, according to documents declassified on Wednesday. The Spanish government declassified a trove of more than 40 documents, including internal alerts, intelligence reports, charts and communications from multiple law enforcement and intelligence agencies. One urgent memo sent by the National Intelligence Center to authorities in Ceuta on the day before the incident warned of "several calls to carry out entries into Ceuta." "There are two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers," the declassified memo read, “just to give you an idea of its scale." CENIF, a border division of the National Police, also published a warning about the social media groups a day before the incident. "Internal communications have been detected in migrant groups in which they are trying to organize mass entries on the night of 29/07/2026," a document from CENIF read. Sanchez downplays level of warning Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the documents prove his government had not been warned of the magnitude of the crisis that was about to unfold. He said the National Intelligence Center only alerted authorities in Ceuta and not the military or Ministry of Defense. "This is understandable because, with the information available at the time, no one could have foreseen the migration crisis that unfolded on the 30th and 31st," Sanchez said on social media. "No competent body did so. Neither in Spain nor in the EU." EU to fund Ceuta border enhancements The European Union (EU) on Wednesday announced that it would grant Spain some €115 million ($130 million) in emergency financial aid to help bolster the bloc's external borders and return thousands of individuals who overwhelmed authorities in the country's North African exclave Ceuta in late July. Spain initially requested the funding on August 24. Brussels said the funds would help finance "measures to enhance border surveillance, border protection and security-related infrastructure" such as thermal cameras, floating buoy systems and underwater drones: "It will also serve to set up facilities for the screening of migrants, as well as to support returns of those who remain illegally in Ceuta." "The situation in Ceuta has put pressure on our external borders," said European Commission Vice President Henna Virkkunen. "Our message remains clear: We are committed to combating illegal migration and ensuring the swift return of those who remain illegally in Ceuta." What happened in Ceuta? On July 30 and 31, images of migrants storming the borders of the exclave sent shockwaves across the EU and beyond as more than 72,000 individuals crossed into Spanish territory from Morocco. Scores of migrants died in their attempt to reach EU territory, most by drowning. Although most of those who breached Ceuta's borders have been returned, thousands remain, many of them unaccompanied minors living in dire conditions. The incident caused a major rift among EU member states, most publicly between Spain's left-wing government and Italy's far-right leadership. Although Sanchez has said that there is "no solid proof" that Morocco was to blame for the incident, Madrid's top criminal court on Monday opened an investigation into whether African authorities had facilitated the illegal rush. Edited by: Sean Sinico If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: EU proposes more restrictions for Airbnb, holiday rentals
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.02
Airbnb and other companies providing short-term home rentals could face tighter restrictions after the European Commission proposed new rules on Wednesday to help tackle housing shortages in tourist hotspots. A surge in short-term holiday rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing and a spike in housing prices in many of Europe's most popular tourist destinations, prompting residents to protest in recent years . What do we know about the EU's affordable housing proposal? The EU's executive branch unveiled the measures as part of an "affordable housing" package, which will allow local authorities to limit short-term rentals to address what European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera described as a "terrible crisis." "When the market fails to deliver something as fundamental as an affordable home, public authorities have a responsibility to act," the Spanish politician said. The measures seek to harmonize rules across the bloc, after attempts to crack down on Airbnb-style rentals by authorities in cities such as Paris, Berlin and Barcelona, among others, were met with legal challenges by rental and tourism companies. The European Commission's Affordable Housing Act — which still needs to be approved by EU legislators and EU member states — would provide cities with legal support by clarifying when local authorities can act against housing companies without breaking EU single market rules. Under the proposal, city and local authorities would be allowed to limit short-term and holiday rentals as well as curb the purchase of property for short-term letting in areas considered to be "under housing stress," the European Commission said. For an area to be defined as "under stress," certain parameters — including the ratio between local housing prices and incomes — would have to be met. Before restrictions can be introduced, cities would have to show that holiday rentals have had a major negative impact on the affordability or availability of housing for at least three years. The proposed legislation will not impact landlords renting out their primary residence for short-term periods. The Commission also recommended that authorities free up land for more housing and modernize planning and construction of new homes to address housing shortages. How have rental companies reacted? CCIA Europe, a lobbying group that represents Airbnb, among others, said the EU's measures fail to address the need for independent assessment of the restrictions. "Europe will not solve its housing crisis by giving cities an EU framework to restrict short-term rentals and then letting them police their own compliance," CCIA's head of policy Alexandre Roure said in a statement. "Without independent scrutiny or effective redress, this proposal will remain a paper tiger, leaving disproportionate restrictions in place and undermining the legal certainty the Affordable Housing Act is meant to provide," Roure added. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

item.title: Germany's connection to the September 11, 2001 attacks
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.93
"This day has changed the world," German President Johannes Rau said. He had watched in shock as the burning twin towers of the World Trade Center collapsed in New York. Nearly 3,000 people were killed on September 11, 2001, when Islamist terrorists hijacked four passenger planes and turned them into deadly weapons. Eleven Germans among the 9/11 victims Germany’s head of state struggled to find the right words: "We do not know what political or social consequences what happened today will have — what we have watched unfold on our television screens in shock, barely able to comprehend or even reflect on it." It soon emerged that the victims include people from 92 countries, among them 11 Germans. The following day, a rapidly spreading rumor was confirmed: Three of the four suspected hijackers had recently lived in Hamburg. The Islamist terrorists were thought to have been led by Egyptian-born Mohammed Atta, who had come to the northern German city in the early 1990s to study. Mohammed Atta and the Hamburg cell At some point, the young man became radicalized, particularly at Hamburg's Al-Quds Mosque, which was later closed by German security authorities. He spent the final three years of his life in an apartment shared with two other suspected attackers in the Harburg district. The so-called Hamburg terrorist cell was believed to have included six men, among them Moroccan national Mounir al-Motassadeq. He was charged as an accomplice in the world's first trial related to the September 11, 2001, attacks. In 2003, the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court sentenced him to the maximum 15-year prison term for aiding and abetting thousands of murders and for membership in a terrorist organization. German-born Murat Kurnaz held at Guantanamo After serving his sentence, al-Motassadeq was deported to his native Morocco. Another suspected attacker from the circle around pilot Mohammed Atta was Ramzi Binalshibh, who was born in Yemen and had been held without trial at the US detention facility at Guantanamo Bay since 2006. The United States detained hundreds of suspects at the prison, which human rights groups and international bodies have described as contrary to international law. Among them was Murat Kurnaz, who was born in Bremen. He was released in August 2006 after nearly five years without evidence establishing his involvement in the terrorist attacks. Kurnaz later recounted his experience in a book that was adapted into a film in 2013. Frank-Walter Steinmeier before investigative committee Meanwhile, investigative committees in the German Bundestag sought to determine why Kurnaz and other suspects had wrongly come under the scrutiny of US and German intelligence agencies. Among those called to testify was then-Foreign Minister and current German PresidentFrank-Walter Steinmeier. At the center of the inquiry was the question of why German security authorities rejected the possible return in 2002 of the German-born detainee, who held a Turkish passport. "No one doubts, and neither do I, that Mr. Kurnaz suffered terribly in Guantanamo," Steinmeier said. "That is why we also sought to ensure that he was treated in accordance with the rule of law. But at the same time, please understand that we were also obliged to ensure security in our own country." Gerhard Schröder voiced 'unconditional solidarity' The Kurnaz case illustrated the pressure on German policymakers in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks in the US. Chancellor Gerhard Schröder addressed parliament the following day. "Yesterday, September 11, 2001, will go down in history as a dark day for all of us," the Social Democrat said. He said he had expressed to the American president the deeply felt condolences of the entire German people. "I also assured him of Germany's unconditional — I emphasize: unconditional — solidarity," Schröder said. Germany, he added, would offer the US any assistance they requested, "of course, also by identifying and pursuing those responsible for and behind these despicable attacks." Germany's Bundestag passes anti-terror laws Schröder's remarks set the tone and opened the door for a series of tougher laws. Just weeks after the attacks, the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens unveiled its first so-called security package, involving more funding, more personnel as well as greater powers for police and intelligence agencies. Religious organizations that had previously been granted special protection could now be banned like other associations if their activities were directed against the Basic Law, Germany's constitutional order based on freedom and democracy, or if they pursued other criminal aims. Less than four months after the terrorist attacks in the US, Germany's Anti-Terrorism Act took effect. Intelligence agencies were given access to personal data held by banks, airlines and telecommunications companies. Immigration laws were tightened. Through data-mining searches, in which large amounts of data were cross-checked without any specific suspicion, authorities sought to identify so-called sleeper agents — people like Mohammed Atta from the Hamburg terrorist cell, who had not been identified by security agencies in time. The Federal Constitutional Court brought an end to the legally questionable practice. Such searches were permissible only when there was a specific threat, the court said in a 2006 ruling. Seven years later, Germany's highest court also ruled that parts of the country's anti-terrorism database were unconstitutional. Germany joins the war in Afghanistan The Islamist terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, also had far-reaching and lasting military consequences. The US launched attacks on the Taliban in Afghanistan as early as October 2001. The Taliban had refused to hand over Osama bin Laden, the head of the al-Qaeda terrorist network and suspected mastermind of the attacks. Germany joined the US-led war in December 2001. The conflict lasted 20 years and ended in August 2021 with the Taliban's return to power. Around 3,600 soldiers from the international forces were killed, including 59 members of Germany's Bundeswehr. Three German police officers also died. The words spoken by German President Johannes Rau on Sept. 11, 2001, in the aftermath of the Islamist terrorist attacks in the US, still resonate today: "This day has changed the world." This article was originally published in German.

item.title: Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.45
US tech company Google on Wednesday announced that it would be investing €13 billion ($15.1 billion) in AI infrastructure in Finland as well as penning a massive deal to buy nuclear power in the Nordic country over the next two decades. This year, Google parent company Alphabet increased global investment to around $200 billion as it rushes to catch up in the AI race. Wednesday's announced deal is Google's biggest single investment in the EU to date. Since repurposing a former paper mill in the coastal city of Hamina in 2009 and transforming it into a data center, Google has steadily increased its presence in the country. The northern location offers two advantages, cold Arctic temperatures mean it needs less energy to cool energy hungry servers and the fact that Finland only has 6 million residents would seem to provide relief from the growing resistance that such projects are running up against in the US and elsewhere. Google is not alone in looking to chilly Finland with its cheap nuclear, wind and hydroelectric energy supply to expand its business — Microsoft and TikTok parent ByteDance have also set up shop — with dozens of data centers being built in the country over the past few years. Attracting data center investment has been a priority for Finland's right-wing Prime Minister Petteri Orpo as the nation confronts record unemployment and slow economic growth. Google makes big claims about boosting Finnish GDP and creating jobs In a statement, Google said the investment, scheduled to be doled out in 2027 and 2028, will include data centers, electrical grid improvement, and clean energy and battery projects for its chatbot, search and map services. The company claims the investment will pump some €3.6 billion into Finland's GDP and create 37,000 jobs, with 7,000 being permanent and others coming during the construction phase. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo echoed Google's rosy outlook for his country's economy, emphasizing that it would spur further investment while downplaying fears that Google's project could drive up energy prices and gobble up resources."This investment is historical in Finland," said Orpo. "This makes us a front-runner in digitalization and AI." Orpo said Google is, "committed to ensuring that electricity production in Finland remains sufficient and that prices remain under control." The tax-avoiding US company said the deal was, "a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure." "Now we are building more in Hamina, expanding that site on a remarkable level, and we are opening up data center operations in three new locations in the municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala," said Antti Jarvinen, the company's director of operations for Finland. Beyond skyrocketing energy consumption, Finland's data center boom presents a potential security risk Wednesday's deal also includes a purchase agreement for 50% of energy output from one of Finland's two nuclear power plants for the next 22 years according to plant operator Fortum, which will team up with the tech giant to explore new nuclear and renewable projects in the country. Fortum shares jumped 15.5% on news of the deal, pushing them to their highest level in over four years and making the company the biggest winner on European stock exchanges for the day. "We call this BYOP — bring your own power," said Google President and Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat, who noted, "This is Google's first nuclear energy deal outside of the United States." Fortum said the deal would allow it to "continue operating the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant until the end of its operating licenses in 2050," adding that without it, the plant, which currently supplies about 10% of Finland's electricity, would not have been able to continue operations past 2030. Overall, Finland's data center boom is expected to create a massive spike in energy consumption, with network operator Fingrid forecasting a 40% jump over the coming years. Beyond the environmental and energy concerns raised by such deals, Finland's Security and Intelligence Service (SUPO) has also issued explicit warnings that foreign-owned data centers pose potential security risks for the Nordic nation. SUPO is concerned that municipalities may be weighing the economic potential of data centers more heavily than the security risk associated with them, noting that despite data center investments being fundamentally good for Finland there may be concerns if their owners are linked to authoritarian countries like Russia or China. SUPO says authoritarian states may, for instance, try to use Finland to circumvent restrictions and sanctions on technology exports. For example, for advanced chips currently banned from export to China. item.title: PISA 2025 results: Reading and math scores plummet worldwide
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.91
The results of the 2025 PISA study, published on September 8, show a dramatic drop in performance in reading and mathematics around the world. The Program for International Student Assessment, better known as PISA, is a global study that measures how well 15-year-old students can apply their knowledge and skills in reading, mathematics and science to real-life situations. The test is designed to measure problem-solving skills rather than evaluate students on memorized school facts, which means they cannot revise in preparation for it. First administered in 2000, it is considered the world's most influential measure of educational performance. In 2025, more than 760,000 students in 91 countries and economies took the test. The study always includes in its ranking the average of the international group of 38 advanced, high-income countries that are part of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, the OECD. Downward trend in students' performances Between 2015 and 2025, reading skills have seen the most significant decline, decreasing by 28 points in OECD countries, and by 16 points in the other participating countries and economies. Scores in math have dropped by 22 points across the OECD on average, compared to a decline of 8 points in the rest of the world. In science, the focus of the 2025 PISA assessment, a seven-point decline was measured in OECD countries, while the performances in other countries and economies remained broadly stable. Nearly a third of OECD students considered 'low performers' The latest PISA study reveals that around 29% of 15-year-olds in OECD countries are now estimated to be "low performers" across all three subjects. What does this mean? In science, they struggle to interpret simple data or decipher a graph. In reading, they find it hard to find information in simple texts. In mathematics, they might be unable to understand, for example, the relationship between units and price — basic skills needed for grocery shopping. Drop in global reading scores most concerning Across the OECD, reading scores fell by 25 score points on average. The study points out that 20 score points are about equivalent to a year of learning. This implies that most 15-year-old students were performing at the level typically expected of 14-year-olds. Among the OECD countries, the drops were most extreme in Iceland and Slovenia, with scores going down by more than 50 points. Reading scores improved in five countries only: Qatar (up 11 points), Brunei Darussalam (18), Cambodia (26), the Philippines (27) and Zambia (50). Even though these education systems are still below the OECD average, they "deserve recognition for achieving measurable gains despite the broader global decline," notes the study. Not all schools are equal in Germany In some countries, such as Iceland, Cambodia and Finland, for example, there is very little variation in performance among schools, showing less than 10% overall variation in student achievement. But in 10 countries, including Germany, differences among schools account for at least 50% of the total variation in performance. The study notes that these countries' systems presumably have schools reserved for higher-achieving students, leaving disproportionately large numbers of lower-achieving students enrolled in the other institutions. For the authors of the PISA study presentation, this is a problem that needs to be taken seriously: "Where such academic segmentation compounds with social background, it can amplify inequalities, producing pockets of excellence while failing to ensure consistent learning outcomes across the education system as a whole." Germany's PISA shocks The very first PISA study was held in the year 2000. As one of the 31 participating countries, Germany was shocked to discover that its 15-year-olds scored below the international average. In the last PISA test, held in 2022 and published in 2023, the scores of German students had dropped to a new low. In the latest study, scores have plunged even deeper. Between 2022 and 2025, reading scores plummeted by 15 points and math scores by 11 points, while science scores have gone down by seven. The top six rankings in reading skills are held by Asian countries. Germany barely remains above the OECD average, coming in 24th. The United States comes in 13th position, Poland ranks 14th and Turkey 18th. In math, Germany is below the OECD average, coming in 26th, just a rank above the United States. All top seven positions are held by Asian countries, followed by Estonia in the 8th spot. In science, Germany is only two score points above the OECD average, ranking 23rd. Turkey made important progress in this field, now ranking 19th, with an increase of 18 score points since the 2022 study. Why is educational performance falling globally overall? The data itself cannot explain the decline in reading skills, but the authors of the study note that while school closures due to COVID-19 may be one factor, there is no direct relationship between how long schools closed during the pandemic and the students' performances in reading. There was already a downward trend in many countries long before the pandemic struck, the study notes. These long-term declines in skills "suggest deeper structural issues within education systems, with challenges at the school and system level," according to the study. These challenges include the impact of digital distractions on students and growing disinterest towards reading books. AI has had an immediate impact on learning. The 2025 PISA study asked students about their use of AI in schoolwork; more than 40% said they used it to draft texts for writing assignments once or twice a week, or even every day. Students who reported using AI chatbots got lower scores in science, on average, than those who didn't use AI. "Overall, the data suggests weaknesses in how education systems are adapting to social, technological and economic change," states the study's summary. "Looking ahead, the challenge for policymakers is not simply recovering lost ground, but to ensure schools meet the rapidly changing demands of the world. As PISA shows, it is not an easy task." While waiting for policymakers to react, the study suggests that parents can contribute to children's potential by being supportive and curious about their studies and helping them develop positive attitudes towards school. "Even something as simple as asking children what they learned or did at school, about once a week or more, is associated with an average 26-point increase in science performance, after accounting for socio-economic status." Edited by: Brenda Haas

item.title: Norway's PM: Zelenskyy's plane almost hit by drone
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.75
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said on Wednesday that a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo for the funeral of Norway's recently deceased King Harald V was almost hit by a drone. "His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in," Store told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK, adding that Zelenskyy had left Norway for Canada, where he would meet with leaders in Ottawa. Store provided no further details about the incident, which reportedly happened on Tuesday, as Zelenskyy was en route from Moldova to Norway. Moldova's government spokesperson said later on Wednesday that the flight was delayed when the country's airspace was closed over a drone alert. The spokesperson said in a statement that Zelenskyy's plane was able to depart after a Russian drone came down on Moldovan territory. The Ukrainian president arrived in Oslo on Tuesday evening. In the Norwegian capital, he held talks with Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide and Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg regarding military aid, including air-defense support, as well as civilian assistance. On Wednesday, Zelenskyy then joined other foreign dignitaries at the funeral of King Harald. Russian drone in Moldova Meanwhile, neither Ukrainian authorities nor Zelenskyy himself have commented on the drone incident. A claim that Zelenskyy was at risk was described as "exaggerated" by the source. According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) — a US think tank — a Russian drone flew in Moldovan and Romanian airspace for about an hour on Tuesday. The ISW said the defense ministries of Moldova and Romania both reported that a Shahed drone entered Moldovan airspace from Ukraine, flew over Romania, and then returned to Moldova, where it crashed. However, it is unclear whether this was the same drone mentioned by Store and the Moldovan government spokesperson. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko Don't let the algorithm hide the news.
