item.title: China: English to be removed as a graded core subject?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.73
From business and academia to social media and entertainment — English is considered the dominant global language. One in five people on Earth actively uses this lingua franca. In China, a mathematics professor specializing in vector algebra is now challenging this dominance in no uncertain terms. Tang Jiafeng believes that English should be abolished as a core subject in elementary schools, secondary schools and universities. Tang is convinced that no other country in the world has placed as much importance on English as China has. "Our children desperately begin learning English even before they have properly mastered their native language. Yet we are a civilization that dates back thousands of years. English is just a tool. It's enough to be able to use it. The tradition of revering and emulating Western cultures must come to an end," Tang says in social media. English as a required subject starting in third grade English is considered difficult in China, since the Chinese language does not use an alphabetic script. It is a required subject starting in third grade. It is graded on par with Chinese and mathematics on the entrance exam for secondary schools, the central exam after 9th grade, and the high school graduation exam. A maximum of 150 points can be earned on the latter. "How many resources and how much time do our children, parents and schools invest in a subject that is completely irrelevant to the majority of people in their future professional lives?" the mathematician asks, explaining his position. He became well-known because many of his students achieved full scores on state math exams; in the class of 2011, six students from a single class did so. Does AI reduce the need to learn English? Tang's opinion spread quickly online. "Why cram for English when artificial intelligence can translate everything in seconds?" comments a user from Beijing. Another suggestion from the southern province of Guangdong is to at least adjust the scoring — for example, to 120 points instead of 150 on the high school graduation exam. Many parents invest in private tutoring that focuses specifically on exam questions. In addition, all bachelor's students must pass the English exam before being admitted to master's programs. Tang suspects that this could cause many young talents in the natural sciences to fail, even though they have great potential to become top researchers. Could less English hurt China's competitiveness There is no question that English is also important for STEM subjects. Research on future-oriented topics is typically published in English. There are fears circulating online that cutting back on English instruction could lead to a decline in China's competitiveness. A prominent advocate for English as a required subject is Hu Xijin, former editor-in-chief of the state-run "Global Times," who has previously drawn attention primarily for his nationalistic statements. Hu emphasizes that foreign language skills are of great importance for every global citizen, "because we live primarily in the present," alluding to a debate over the ungraded history exam. "This present is shaped by globalization. China's opening up is not only state policy but also expands people's scope of action as well as the range of their diverse material and immaterial interests in life." Hu went on to say that connections to the outside world should not, therefore, be compared to intellectual ties to ancient history. "Forcibly pitting them against each other — by asking whether foreign languages or traditional Chinese culture are more important — runs the risk of setting the wrong priorities and unnecessarily politicizing public discussions." For him, an open engagement with the outside world is the top priority. English as a core subject also promotes equal opportunity, he noted, as it gives children in rural areas access to this important foreign language and thus to the world. How China is changing foreign language education Even Chinese universities specializing in foreign languages are feeling the pressure to adjust their educational goals and prepare incoming freshmen for future job markets. For example, fewer and fewer high school graduates are interested in German language studies, explains a university professor from Beijing who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity. The new curriculum at Beijing Foreign Studies University has adopted a "foreign language plus major" model: English combined with law, information technology, or economics. Similar cultural struggles already took place during the Self-Strengthening Movement in the late 19th century under the Qing Dynasty. "Learn the superior skills from abroad so that you can later conquer the outside world," said Wei Yuan, a court scholar at the time. Learning from abroad simply works better in the language used there. Even though it may be becoming apparent that, in some areas, other countries are more interested in learning from China— as is already the case today, for example in battery technology for the automotive industry, and humanoid robotics. This article was originally published in German.

item.title: EU, UK express dismay over Mladic funeral in Serbia
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.73
Both the EU and UK on Tuesday expressed dismay over the funeral in Belgrade, Serbia of late war criminal Ratko Mladic a day prior. Thousands of people, including at least six Serbian ministers, attended the event on Monday which was seen as glorifying Mladic. He received military honors at the funeral, with the head of Serbia's Orthodox Church presiding over the ceremony. The Bosnian Serb commander died last month at The Hague, where he had been imprisoned for life. Mladic was convicted in 2017 of genocide, having orchestrated the July 1995 Srebrenica massacre, where 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed. Mladic, called the "Butcher of Bosnia" by some international press, is a revered as a war hero by many Serbian nationalists in both Serbia and Bosnia. EU leader call Mladic state funeral 'deeply regrettable' EU leaders condemned the funeral, with the bloc weighing an official response to the event. "The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa said in statements posted on X. "They demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe's recent history and contradict the values underpinning Serbia's path towards the European Union," they added. A European Commission spokeperson, in comments to German news agency DPA, said next steps were being evaluated. EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas added: "Serbia's path into the European Union requires an unequivocal commitment in fundamental European values and historical truth." Serbia first applied for EU membership in 2009. Serbia's EU candidacy was confirmed by the European Council in 2012. UK summons Serbian envoy The UK, meanwhile, summoned Serbia's charge d'affaires in response to the funeral. "As a military commander, Mladic presided over crimes that are among the worst committed in Europe since the Second World War," the British Foreign Office said in a statement. "The thoughts of the UK Government are with Mladic's victims and their families. They deserve respect, compassion and accountability, not efforts to rewrite proven history," the statement added. The UK said that the "glorification of a convicted war criminal directly undermines trust, fuels division, and is incompatible with the process of reconciliation within Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region." Bosnia expels Serbian diplomats, says Belgrade crossed 'red line' In its reaction to the funeral, neighboring Bosnia expelled two Serbian diplomats, saying Serbia crossed a "red line" in its display of reverence for Mladic. "They crossed every red line with what they did yesterday, the day before, and in the days leading up to the reception," Bosnian Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic told a Sarajevo press event. Konakovic had also said he would withdraw most staff from the Bosnian Embassy in Belgrade in an effort to reduce ties to "the lowest possible level" Serbian President Aleksander Vucic was not present at Mladic's funeral, although his son Danilo, did attend the event. Vucic rejected allegations that Mladic was being glorified at the funeral and said the event was put together by Mladic's family rather than the state. The controversial funeral comes ahead of snap elections next month. Serbia has faced a political crisis in the past two years triggered by the collapse of a concrete canopy at a railway station in Novi Sad. Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Norway's King Harald V laid to rest in state funeral
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.68
A 21-gun salute rang out over Oslo on Wednesday afternoon as the coffin of Norway's King Harald V left the royal palace for the city's Lutheran cathedral. Thousands of people lined the streets to say goodbye to the king. Norway then observed a minute of silence to start the funeral service. The procession and funeral brought an end to 13 days of national mourning following the death of the well-liked monarch at the age of 89. "He struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth," Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said in his eulogy. "He made Norway greater. He spoke of a 'we' in Norway where everyone is there for each other." After the ceremony, his casket was moved to its final resting place at the royal palace chapel. A private ceremony just for family followed. Who attended the funeral? The funeral was attended by heads of state and government from all over the world. They included the UK's Prince William and Princess Anne, Japan's Crown Prince Fumihito and his wife Princess Kiko, Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia, as well as fellow Scandinavian royals from Denmark and Sweden. Other leaders such as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier were also attending. Indeed, flags were flown at half-mast in Berlin's government in honor of Harald, whose 35-year-reign made him well-known and respected across Europe. Harald's son King Haakon VIII was be there alongside his family including his mother Queen Sonja and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit. Controversially, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship was also expected to be at the funeral. Marius Borg Hoiby's participation in an earlier part of the official mourning drew an outcry in Norway, as he was recently convicted of rape and domestic violence and is under house arrest. Edited by: Wesley Rahn If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Syria arms depot explosion kills at least 14
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.65
Syrian authorities reported that at least 14 people were killed and another 11 wounded on Wednesday as a result of an explosion at a temporary site used to store weapons and remnants of the country's long-running civil war. The explosion took place near the city of Sarmada in the northwestern Idlib province. What do we know about the explosion? Syria's Defense Ministry said the weapons and war remnants were being stored termporarily at the site before being transported elsewhere. It said that some of its personnel were among those wounded. The explosion in an area full of volatile materials led to secondary explosions and fires that hampered the emergency response. Smoke billowed from the blast site for some time on Wednesday. "The toll from the explosion in a temporary storage for collecting weapons and war remnants near the city of Sarmada ... registered 14 killed and 11 injured in a preliminary count," the Idlib health department said. Authorities have not yet said what caused the explosion. It was the second fatal incident of its kind in Idlib province this month. On September 1, five people were killed and others were wounded when a vehicle carrying ammunition exploded in Binnish. Syria only recently emerged from more than a decade of civil war, when forces loyal to new President Ahmed al-Sharaa ousted Bashar Assad and took control of Damascus. Idlib was one of the hardest-hit regions in the country during the war. item.title: Switzerland: Two killed in power plant explosion
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.28
Two workers were killed in an explosion at a hydroelectric power plant in the village of Piotta in southern Switzerland on Wednesday, according to local authorities. Police say a fire was reported at the Ritom Hydroelectric Station in the canton of Ticino around 9:30 a.m. (0730 GMT). The blaze trapped two workers inside. Shortly thereafter, an explosion rocked the plant, severely damaging the building and gravely injuring the men, both of whom died from their injuries shortly thereafter. Authorities say one of the men was a a 55-year-old Swiss citizen, the other has yet to be identified. State prosecutors have launched an investigation into the cause of the deadly incident. The facility, which is owned by Swiss rail carrier SBB, is currently undergoing renovations as part of a plan to reconfigure the 100-year-old site. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Philippines: Several killed, dozens missing after fire on ferry
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.19
At least five people were killed and 87 are missing after a ferry caught fire in the Philippine province of Palawan, the Coast Guard said on Thursday. The incident aboard the MV June Aster occurred on Wednesday evening about 2.2 kilometers (1.3 miles) off the shore of the municipality of Coron, where it was headed after departing from Baseco in Manila. Coast Guard officials said 42 people had been rescued, including 38 passengers and four crew members. Footage released by the Coast Guard showed the vessel engulfed in flames, and bodies placed in body bags. The ship's manifest listed 134 people onboard, including 117 passengers and 17 crew members, according to the Philippine Coast Guard. "Based on the data we have right now on rescued (42) and the casualties, we still have 87 people who are unaccounted for," Coast Guard Captain Noemi Cayabyab said on Thursday, adding that the figures could change as search and rescue operations continued. item.title: Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.12
Iranian authorities have launched a clampdown on cafes in the capital, Tehran, in recent months, suspecting them of fostering anti-government sentiment and facilitating protests. According to the human rights organization HRANA, at least seven cafes and restaurants were shut down on July 19 alone for allegedly failing to comply with mandatory hijab rules. Previously, some media outlets, including Javan, a newspaper affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have described cafes as "gathering places for protesters" who, in their view, pose a threat to "national security." Most recently, the "Vanak Park" cafes in Tehran were sealed, resulting in at least 200 people losing their jobs. Crackdown on cafes Authorities believe cafes, because of their widespread presence and popularity, could play a role in organizing mass protests. The government's fears are rooted in the latest wave of protests in Iran, which began on December 28, 2025, and grew into the country's largest uprising since the 1979 Islamic Revolution. Saediniya, a well-known cafe chain with 10 branches in Iran, closed its branches on this day in support of calls for strikes. It was subsequently accused of engaging in "propaganda against the state." Iran's Supreme Court has now upheld the sentence of Sadegh Saedinia, the owner of the cafe chain, to 12 years and six months in prison, along with the confiscation of his assets. He was arrested over his support for the protests, and all branches of his cafe chain were confiscated and shut down by judicial order. Other cafes, including "Lamiz" and "Voria," faced a broadly similar fate. Voria is owned by a prominent Iranian footballer. Both were sealed by judicial order because of their indirect support for calls to protest. Cafe closures have not been confined to periods of protest, however, and the practice continues. The rise of the cafe culture Tehran has seen a surge in the number of cafes over the past decade, rising from around 300 in the early 2010s to as many as 4,000 now, according to various estimates. Some experts attribute the growing number to changes in urban lifestyles in recent years. They see this as more than the expansion of a particular type of business and describe it as a sign of wider social and cultural changes within Iranian society. "The explosive growth of cafes in society can, to some extent, be seen as a social response to living in a state of chronic crisis," Saba Alaleh, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst whose work focuses on political and social issues, told DW's Persian service. "In such circumstances, people are not simply looking to consume or be entertained. They are looking for a place to temporarily distance themselves from the pressures of everyday life," she said. "In this sense, the cafe becomes a third space. It is neither home nor the workplace, but a space between the two where people can briefly step away from their everyday roles and pressures, connect with others, and feel that life is still somewhat manageable and normal." The cafe trend has become particularly popular among Gen Z, who are bearing the brunt of runaway inflation and steep living costs in Iran. "The young people who gather in these cafes do not necessarily come from affluent backgrounds," Nasser, a cafe owner in Tehran, told DW. "In many parts of Tehran, young people from the middle class also meet at cafes, and many of our customers belong to this group." The political role of cafes Even before the latest bout of nationwide protests that began at the end of last year, shutting down cafes was common practice for the Iranian government. Most of these crackdowns and closures, however, were carried out under the pretext of enforcing compulsory hijab. The protests that began in late December 2025 changed that, with cafes becoming the target more often and for varied reasons. "They shut down our cafe on the pretext that we had served customers who were not wearing the hijab, but that is only an excuse," Nasser said. "Outside, on the streets of Tehran, women and girls have effectively abandoned the compulsory hijab, yet the government expects us not to allow them into the cafe," he added. Maintaining control over social spaces Alaleh said the issue is no longer simply about cracking down on women for not wearing the hijab. "Authoritarian governments generally seek to control the flow of information, social interactions and the organization of citizens," she pointed out. "Any space beyond the direct supervision of those in power that allows trust, dialogue and social ties to develop can weaken part of the government's monopoly over the social sphere." The expert said the crackdown on cafes and cafegoers is part of the government's efforts to preserve its monopoly over social spaces. She underlined that to a security apparatus, even a group of young people casually sitting together can represent the emergence of an independent social network outside the formal structures of power. "The broader and more deeply rooted these independent networks become, the more difficult it is for the government to maintain exclusive control over the public sphere," added Alaleh. Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

item.title: Conspiracy theories can provide answers but not peace
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.11
Psychology is not an exact science. That may irk a few researchers in the field. But it is important to mention upfront: Researching the psychology of conspiracy theories — why people are drawn to believing them and the effect they have on those people — is a complicated field of research, and conclusions are difficult to derive. That is due, in part, to one of the basic problems with psychology, whether it's in treatment or in research, and that is that it relies on people's self-awareness. If we take the example of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, some people continue to maintain it was "inside job," orchestrated by a secretive and powerful club of evil doers in the US government, intent on controlling citizens' lives by fear. And that may be true. But it may also be true that you, as a believer in such a theory, have always felt powerful people — your parents or teachers — have controlled and curtailed your agency in life. You may even have a false memory of how the terrorist attacks evolved on that day in 2001. Then, if someone asked you, "What really happened?", could you really say it for sure? I couldn't. Self-report data are an issue in conspiracy research Whether as patients or participants in a study, we may be asked to "self-report" — to look inside ourselves and express how we feel and why. Self-reporting is an established way of measuring conspiracies, said Neil Dagnall, a professor of psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University, in an interview with DW. But self-report data are "not perfect," he added. They can be difficult data to handle because each judgment a person makes about themselves is relative, inherently subjective and open to outside influence and bias. People's answers can change from day-to-day, especially when they involve emotions or feelings about mental state, depending on a multitude of events and experiences in our lives. In addition, there is no common scale. Say, for example, you and a friend were asked, "Are you happy?" You may both say "yes," but your reasons for doing so may be completely different and be subject to different variables. The same goes for a question like, "Do you believe in conspiracy theories?" "The judgment I'm making is a relative one. What's my norm? Am I comparing it to my friends who don't believe in conspiracies, or am I in a group of people who do believe in conspiracies? We're always making relative judgments about our psychological propensities," said Dagnall. Which suggests we're unlikely to ever get a definitive answer. Self-report data suggest correlations, not causation. In a study on conspiratorial beliefs and well-being, which Dagnall co-authored and published in May 2026, "self-report data" was specifically highlighted as a limitation. This makes it very difficult to assess whether "conspiracy belief" or "conspiracy ideation" is good or bad for people and their sense of well-being. Especially as people who seek and believe in conspiracy theories often start out with a skewed view of reality. Observing behavior can offer clues There are ways of "triangulating" self-report data, as the authors of the study put it, to get a more reliable, objective reading of a person's emotional or psychological state. For example, psychologists use behavioral observations, like measuring heart rate variability or Galvanic Skin Responses such as the electrical conductance of a person's skin, which is affected by sweating under stress. You can also retest participants' self-reported data, and therefore its reliability, by asking the same questions at different points in time. But there is another factor that complicates research into the psychology of conspiracy theories, and that is that they, and people who believe in them, are more common than we like to think or admit (even when we believe them ourselves). "The idea that people who believe in conspiracies in general populations are remarkable or different is not true," said Dagnall. The truth: 'conspiracies theories are common' Most of us, at some point in our lives, are bound to see something strange or stressful in society and question whether we, as individuals or as a member of a group, accept the accepted truth of how that thing or event came about. It can be a healthy sign of a questioning mind. There are positive examples of conspiracy theories that happened to kickstart investigations that then revealed the horrible truth of government corruption. Take Partygate during the COVID pandemic in the United Kingdom or — the mother of all conspiracies — Watergate during the Nixon Administration in the United States. And there are other conspiracy theories, such as the one that nobody has ever landed on the moon, which you can either take seriously or laugh about. It all comes down to "the degree to which we engage in conspiracies generally, and the extent to which they interfere and disrupt our everyday lives," said Dagnall. For Dagnall, who doesn't believe in the 1969 moon landing, it doesn't seem to disrupt his daily life — at least, that is what he self-reported to DW. But for some people, conspiracy theories are disruptive and can lead to a sustained sense of dissatisfaction. "Ample studies suggest that exposure to conspiracy theories or belief in them might lead to more negative emotions, heightened anxiety or even paranoid thoughts," said Zuzanna Molenda, a researcher at the Polish Academy of Sciences and lead-author of a 2023 study on emotion dysregulation and belief in conspiracy theories. Some people may be primed to more readily believe in conspiracy theories because they generally struggle to deal with psychological threat and distress. When they then seek answers in conspiracy theories, their pre-existing negative psychology may be enhanced. "If anything, the available evidence suggests that rather than help people manage difficult emotions, conspiracy beliefs may be accompanied by or contribute to further distress," wrote Molenda in an email to DW. No long-term benefit from conspiracy belief There may be some psychological benefit to conspiracy theories, said Molenda, but only in the short term. "Conspiracy beliefs can provide people with a sense of explanation and understanding when events feel uncertain or difficult to make sense of. For some people, they might also be a source of entertainment and fun. For others, they can provide a sense of belonging and connection with others who share the same beliefs, and they can be an important part of social identity," Molenda said. But these potential benefits do not necessarily translate into better well-being in the longer term, said Molenda. In the end, we're all searching for meaning and purpose in life. If we find a satisfactory answer, it gives us something that psychologists call presense — a direction in life, and that is good. But if your search only leads to more uncertainty, more anxiety and more doubt in your purpose in life, then that's bad. "And people who believe in conspiracies are asking questions but not getting answers," said Dagnall. Edited by: Kristie Pladson

item.title: Oil prices rise as Middle East conflict escalates
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.00
Oil crude prices topped $100 (about €86) a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July amid concerns over oil supplies due to the conflict in the Middle East. "The move towards and back above $100 Brent is reflecting a market that increasingly must change its view on how long the Middle East crisis will continue to curb supply from the region," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at the Danish Saxo Bank. The attacks on Saudi energy facilities by the Iranian-backed Houthisthreaten oil shipments on the Red Sea. This has been a key alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz path. Meanwhile, the US attacked Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and in the Strait of Hormuz. "Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies," CENTCOM said in a statement. Runing out of stock Since the conflict in the Middle East started, oil exports have been reduced significantly, making some countries turn to their reserves. The US has reported its lowest oil reserve since 1982, holding 289.7 million barrels. Former US President Joe Biden and President Donald Trump have used the reserve to cushion consumer prices amid the crisis. The new price of the barrel is still below the peak reached early this year. In April, Brent jumped to $126 a barrel. Experts believe this is a big risk to a market with little room for capacity to absorb new disruptions occasioned by the war. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Syria: How the 'house of sisters' threat split society
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.92
A knock on the door, a muted threat and then they made the decision to leave the country, says Layla, a math teacher and mother-of-three in her 40s. Until recently, Layla — who didn't want DW to use her full name for security reasons — was living in Damascus, Syria's capital. She and her family are Alawites, the same religious sect as former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad, who are often targeted because they're seen as Assad's allies. "But we never supported him, his father killed members of my family. We hated him actually," she told DW. Still, she describes feeling fearful when rebel groups entered Damascus in 2024 for the first time after the fall of the Assad regime, calling them "extremists." At first, she and her husband decided to stay in Syria. But then a stranger came to the door. "He told me 'we know your daughter plays piano and has dance lessons. You should stop that. If you don't, maybe we will take her to the house of the sisters," Layla recounts. In conservative Islamic circles, women playing music and dancing for an audience is frowned upon. And Layla had heard about the so-called "house of the sisters" — she had read online it was a place where Syrian women from other sects were forced to convert to Islam. A few days later, the family decided to leave the country. They are now in Lebanon. "I just don't want my children to grow up that way," Layla explains. What is the 'house of sisters'? Headlines about the "house of sisters" first really made waves in Syria in May after an Alawite university student Batoul Alloush, 21, was reported missing by her family, possibly kidnapped, only to turn up later wearing religious clothing and saying she left her family in order to convert to Islam. There were already other stories of missing women, including from the Alawite minority. Reham Suleiman, a psychologist who works for the United Nations and with the Alawite community, told DW she has firsthand knowledge of several cases of kidnapping. "And it’s not just one incident or coincidence," she says. It is clear some of women were kidnapped for ransom money, revenge or forced marriage. But other cases were apparently resolved when, for example, the women said they had been visiting friends, wanted to escape their families or had run away to a lover. Alloush herself said she wished to convert to Islam and leave her family. Her parents insist she's been drugged or coerced. Organizations like Amnesty International and the UN's Commission of Inquiry on Syria say the cases — which number between 40 and 60 — have not been fully investigated. A political football Syrian authorities did look into the "house of sisters." A spokesperson for Syria's Minister of Social Affairs, Hind Kabawat, told DW that the ministry has not licensed any facility with that name and that any unlicensed centers of this nature would be shut down. Syrian fact-checking organizations like Verify-Sy found that pictures of the supposed "house of sisters" building were created with AI. "A constant stream of unverified claims circulates on a daily basis concerning alleged kidnappings and killings, arrests and cases of torture in detention facilities," a spokesperson from Verify-Sy told DW. "Verifying many of these is challenging when evidence available through open sources is scarce, contradictory or otherwise insufficient." So whether the "house of sisters" exists in some form is unclear. But real or not, some groups appear to have instrumentalized it for their own agenda anyway, independent media outlet Shaam News Network, or SNN, wrote recently. "Despite the absence of any physical evidence … social media platforms and pages began circulating 'the house' as an established fact," SNN wrote. "And it gradually became the focus of broader narratives about the 'organized kidnapping' of Alawite women." International influencers A private organization called the Syrian Investigation Mechanism, or SIM, founded in May 2026, links the "house of sisters" to a Muslim organization that proselytizes to gain new converts. SIM claimed the missing women were coerced into converting and held in "the house." In an interview on YouTube, SIM director Yasir Saleti, who is based in Brandenburg, Germany, claims this is evidence of "demographic engineering." SIM did not reply to DW's requests for further comment. A Berlin-based organization, the Union of Syrian Alawites in Europe, or USAE, has also repeatedly posted about the "house of sisters." On his personal Facebook page, Muaiad Ibrahim, who is listed as USAE's deputy director in official court documents, regularly criticizes the new Syrian government and recently expressed support for Syria's highest religious scholar under the Assad regime, Ahmed Hassoun. In late August, Hassoun was sentenced to life in prison after being convicted of inciting civil war and complicity in intentional killing. Other recently founded overseas organizations — including some that claim they have a network of millions of human rights advocates but link to incomplete websites — have also repeatedly disseminated stories about the "house of sisters." Arab investigative journalism outfit DARAJ notes some of these organizations have been criticized for their apparent support of the Assad regime. The damage done? "This kind of information ebbs and flows, but it does have a real impact and its quite powerful," says Gregory Waters, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, who's traveled extensively in Syria and monitors events on his site, Syria Revisited. "It has the political intent to isolate Alawites, to make them fearful and keep them from engaging with the government, with [Syrian] Sunnis, and maybe to some extent, pull them towards insurgent [anti-government] networks." Online propaganda feeds on real events within minority communities, adding to their existing fears, he says. Verify Sy conducts a monthly audit of online disinformation, and researchers there say incitement is the second most common objective. Waters says Syrian authorities have been trying to rein in local influencers who spread disinformation, although obviously they can't impact those based overseas. Like anywhere else in the world, you'll get a wide spectrum of opinions within every Syrian community, Waters notes. "There are there those who will insist that there's a program of ethnic cleansing, and there are others who say life is fine, we are fully integrated into the state." Although it depends which part of the country you're looking at, he doesn't think relations between different communities are getting worse. "In Syria, everything is unique to its local environment," Waters explains. "So in some places, we could say that walls between communities have hardened over the past two years and little progress has been made in reducing that. But even so, the walls are not getting higher." Stabilization first "Right now, generally speaking, the government in Damascus is busy establishing institutions, taking control of the security situation and trying to stabilize the country," argues Naseef Naeem, research director at the Berlin-based Candid Foundation, which consults on Syrian affairs. But sooner or later, Syria is going to need more of a national dialogue between different community groups, he says. In the meantime, both he and Waters believe the Syrian economy, devastated after years of war, could hold the key to better relations. "As soon as the economic recovery really gets underway, many of these phenomena will gradually disappear," Naeem told DW. For example, Waters says, over summer, a lot of domestic tourists, many of them Sunni, made their way to the Syrian coast, an area where many Alawites live. "There was a massive tourism boom," Waters explains. "Everybody's interacting and I've heard from friends there that there wasn't harassment, no violence. The government and security authorities really emphasized supporting the tourism industry in coastal areas this year and it's had a really positive impact." Those kinds of inter-community contacts in real life "help reduce the impact of disinformation campaigns and the level of fear," he concludes. Edited by: K. Hairsine Editor's note: The spelling of Yasir Saleti's name has been corrected. We regret the error.

item.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.90
In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades. The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species, which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in illegally caught eels. "So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre, who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous." Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed. "The situation is so bad that we have to act on everything," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI. Eel smuggling as lucrative as drugs Part of what makes European eels so vulnerable is their remarkable life cycle, which was, until relatively recently, a source of mystery. Scientists now know adult eels migrate thousands of kilometers from European rivers to the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic, their only known spawning grounds. They breed and then die, leaving their larvae to drift to Europe. By the time they reach rivers, they've transformed into tiny, transparent "glass eels." Today, the number of glass eels reaching the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways is only around 12% of what it was before the 1980s, Diaz says. The young glass eels conservationists are trying to protect are the most valuable in the illegal trade, fetching up to €9,000 ($10,400) per kilogram. "You can compare it with drug trafficking. Every year they seize tons of illegally caught eel in Europe," said Eizaguirre. "The big business lies in trafficking them to Asia," adding that the huge profits and comparatively small fines for smaller infractions by local fishers make the risk worth it. However, when criminal organizations are involved, penalties can be substantial with fines up to 6 times the value of illegally smuggled eel. Demand in countries such as China, South Korea and Japan is driving prices. As is a biological peculiarity: So far, it's been exceedingly difficult to get eels to reproduce in captivity. This means fish farms — where the eels are raised before being sold to premium restaurants — need a steady stream of young from the wild. Sometimes, the same smuggled eels come back to Europe as fillets for the sushi market. Conservationists had hoped pressure on the species would ease when the EU banned export of the species outside the bloc in 2010. Instead, organized crime groups have increasingly muscled in on the market, with the illegal trade now generating an estimated €3 billion in profits in peak years. "Our estimated maximum was always 100 tons of glass eels smuggled annually. That's already around 300 million fish," said Florian Stein, head of policy and science at the German Angling Association. But information from his contacts in the illegal trade have led him to the conclusion that it was a "very conservative estimate." International law enforcement agencies are also cracking down, with Europol's Operation Lake seizing 22 tons of glass eels and arresting 26 suspects between 2024 and 2025. "There has been a lot of pressure from law enforcement throughout Europe," said Interpol's Sanchez Romero. "That's why the criminal groups always look for new routes." Eels smuggled in suitcases along complex routes Stein, who wrote his doctoral dissertation on international eel smuggling and advises the German government, said trafficking has increased since 2020, and illegal trade routes have become more complex. "Ten years ago, Madrid airport was still one of the biggest smuggling hotspots," he added. This was due to its proximity to fishing grounds in northern Spain and Portugal. Increased checks by Spanish authorities on flights to East Asia forced traffickers to adapt. Experts now say a new route running through North Africa via Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal has become increasingly important. Geography is one reason the route is attractive. The Strait of Gibraltar is 14 kilometers at its narrowest point and a busy maritime junction. "We know that many drugs are also transported through this strait," Moroccan investigative journalist Yassir Al-Makhtoum told DW. European eels also inhabit rivers and estuaries in Morocco. Though the country has banned the export of glass eels smaller than 12 centimeters (4.7 inches), it is building a legal domestic eel trading industry. Experts fear that's acting as a cover for trafficked animals coming in from Europe. From Morocco, smugglers then move eels along numerous routes to Asia. The means are not always sophisticated. Glass eels can be transported in ordinary suitcases on domestic flights. They're placed in bags filled with a little water and insulated to keep their temperature stable. They can survive for up to 48 hours in those conditions. Once in Asia, they go to the fish farms. A species running out of time Eels are an important indicator species for the health of ocean and riverine ecosystems because their long migrations across multiple habitats make them vulnerable to problems that could also harm other species. They also serve as important prey for herons, otters and larger fish. "But the impact of its disappearance is difficult to predict," said marine biologist Diaz. Under EU regulations, member states must undertake measures to allow 40% of adult eels to return to the Sargasso Sea to spawn. Diaz also wants to ensure at least 40% of glass eels make it back from the Sargasso Sea. But European eels are not the only eel species under threat. A proposal to protect all freshwater eel species from illegal and unsustainable trade was rejected at the 2025 CITES wildlife conference. For Stein such protection is key. "The proposal should be on the table again at the next conference. I just don't know how else we can get a handle on this problem," said Stein, adding more lobbying and coalition building is needed to advocate for a ban. “The eel for us is more than just a fish,” said Unai Eizaguirre. “It's been part of our identity for centuries.” For fishermen like him, better protection for the eel represents a chance at a sustainable future. Edited by: Jennifer Collins The research for this story was sponsored by: The Med Mosaic. This article was updated to clarify the fall in volume of glass eels reaching the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways is compared to figures from the 1980s.

item.title: The Coming Risks to Russian Power
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.52
The United States has long viewed Russia as a power in terminal decline. This assessment formed in the 1980s as the Soviet Union began showing clear signs of imperial overstretch, and it congealed after the collapse of first the Warsaw Pact and then the Soviet Union itself. Washington went on to pursue a policy agenda, including NATO enlargement, that treated Russian power and interests as an afterthought, and the long-standing conflict over Ukraine turned dismissiveness into condescension. In March 2014, U.S. President Barack Obama called Russia “a regional power” that was “threatening some of its immediate neighbors, not out of strength but out of weakness.” President Donald Trump shows more fondness for Russian President Vladimir Putin than his predecessors did, but most Russia watchers in the West still dwell on Russia’s lagging technology; its failure to rescue allies in Syria, Venezuela, and Cuba; and what they see as its reduction to a vassal of mighty China. This picture of Russia as feeble and fading may suit the biases of Putin’s many critics, but it is fundamentally at odds with reality: Moscow consistently punches above its weight in global affairs. Thirty-five years after the disintegration of the Soviet Union, Russia remains a nuclear superpower. As during the Cold War, NATO treats it as the benchmark threat around which the alliance plans its forces. An unprecedented wall of Western sanctions has failed to trigger the economic collapse its architects predicted or to erode political and social stability. The effort to isolate Moscow has faltered as well. The Kremlin has skillfully promoted non-Western bodies such as BRICS, a grouping of major emerging economies, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a Eurasian political and security group. In so doing, it has extended its influence over the post-Western order now taking shape. And even though Russia’s economy is far smaller than China’s, the “no limits” partnership between Moscow and Beijing has produced a formidable coalition. This bullish assessment comes with a caveat: it relies on the international conditions that prevail today. Moscow continues to punch above its weight because it is navigating a fragmented, unpredictable world that plays to its strengths. Volatility and instability, active conflicts and arms races across several regions, economic decoupling and the retreat of globalization, the worldwide rise of nationalism and populism, the discounting of soft power and fissures in the Western alliance—all these features of the existing international order work to Moscow’s advantage. The downside risk for Russia is that today’s turmoil and uncertainty may not last. The pendulum is likely to swing back, with global disorder subsiding and the international system consolidating anew. That reversal could come when Trump leaves the White House, especially if his successor restores traditional U.S. support for the transatlantic alliance, multilateralism, and open trade. A planetary shock—accelerating climate change, an out-of-control AI system, or some other surprise—could likewise push states to set aside their current conflicts in favor of closer cooperation. When this change happens—and it will—Russia may find that its time-tested foreign policy and its once reliable but rigid institutions no longer serve it well. THRIVING IN CHAOS The centrifugal trends pulling the international system apart work to Moscow’s advantage. In a fragmented and dangerous world of strongmen, where raw power decides outcomes, Russia’s military heft remains a durable source of strength and influence. Russia is also the only power that can rival the United States in strategic nuclear weapons. China is modernizing and expanding its arsenal, but Beijing will need a long time to catch up with the two superpowers. Russia’s nuclear status has practical effects: it has deterred NATO members from deploying troops to Ukraine, and it gives Moscow powerful diplomatic leverage on arms control, strategic stability and risk reduction, nonproliferation, and the prevention of nuclear terrorism. As for its conventional capabilities, Russia retains a blue-water navy and long-range strike capabilities; only the United States can project power more widely. To be sure, the initial phase of fighting in Ukraine in February 2022 exposed serious weaknesses in the Russian army. But over the four and a half years since, the armed forces have transformed themselves, sharply improving their efficiency and combat power. Moscow now fields one of the world’s strongest militaries and, beyond that, has unique experience in next-generation ground warfare—an edge over almost any other fighting force, the United States included. Ukraine, too, has adapted its forces and tactics to new battle technologies, but it depends on Western support and may not be able to preserve those capabilities once the fighting stops. The accumulated experience of Russia’s armed forces will keep serving Moscow well in an era of frequent conventional wars. A divided, resource-scarce world also magnifies the leverage that Russia’s vast natural endowments give it. Russia is a supplier of oil, natural gas, coal, wheat, fertilizers, uranium, critical metals, diamonds, and other commodities. It regularly plays the role of dealmaker, especially now that supply, not price, is the priority. Europe, for instance, may be weaning itself off Russian fossil fuels, but China’s reliance on those supplies helps offset the asymmetries in the relationship between Moscow and Beijing. The vulnerability of Middle Eastern supply routes during the Iran war has further strengthened Russia’s hand. Perpetual confrontation with the West does not serve Russia’s long-term development. A fiercely competitive, volatile environment also raises the value of Russia’s centralized economic and political systems. In the West, these are often derided as antiquated, inflexible, and harmful to the country’s development. Yet a strong state has helped Russia maintain social, economic, and political stability despite Western pressure and its losses in Ukraine. In an era of heightened polarization, Russia’s centralized, personalized decision-making carries clear advantages over the liberal alternative. Putin governs with little opposition, few divisions within the establishment, and scant pushback from the media, and he can pursue the kind of long-term strategic planning that unpredictable election cycles in the West rule out. The United States, meanwhile, is a divided political mess, presided over by a mercurial president and a dysfunctional Congress. Trump seems not only to respect Putin but also to envy him and his tight grip on Russia. In Britain and France, prime ministers come and go, none able to sustain public confidence. The European Union survives for now, but it makes decisions with excruciating slowness and, within its member states, faces surging support for populist parties eager to topple the bureaucrats in Brussels. As long as the international system favors rivalry over cooperation, security over prosperity, regionalization over globalization, and sovereignty over interdependence, Russia will remain in the top tier of global politics. It will even hold comparative advantages over countries with far greater commercial, financial, and technological capacities. Its rivals will be constrained by their own democratic gridlock and restless electorates. Russia cannot beat the West outright, but it can hold its own and play for a draw—until, that is, today’s competitive and fragmented order gives way to compromise, de-escalation, and stability. THE COMING CALM History moves in cycles, and the current configuration of the international system could prove fleeting. Globalization could return in a new form, and instability could give way to a long stretch of stable peace. The seemingly endless fighting in the Middle East could finally stop; Washington and Beijing might reach a sustainable trade and geopolitical compromise; the European Union may overcome its existential crisis; and a new UN secretary-general could succeed in reviving principles of multilateralism in global affairs. The reversal of the pendulum could begin as early as the coming midterm elections in the United States, if they result in a major defeat for Trump’s supporters on Capitol Hill. In such a world, some of the foreign policy assets Russia now prizes most would begin to lose their value. The softer forms of power, which Russia has long underrated, would matter more. Heavy investment in strategic and conventional forces, for instance, gives Moscow geopolitical heft, but it does nothing to help Russia plug into emerging high-value global supply chains. Were its domestic market as vast as China’s or India’s, Russia could insulate itself from the risks associated with globalization’s return. But its long-term demographic decline forecloses that option. Exporting its way out of hardship by selling even more hydrocarbons won’t work either, given the likely fall in demand for fossil fuels. Competing for large-scale foreign direct investment would be harder still. It requires high levels of interstate trust and transparency, as well as a stable and user-friendly legal framework. The country’s geography offers some advantage. With the world’s longest Arctic coastline, Russia can command a large share of the High North’s resource reserves and of the new shipping routes that will open as the climate warms. But to capitalize on its position as a transit corridor between East Asia and Western Europe, Russia would need long-term, stable partnerships with not only China but also the EU. Such relationships are hard to imagine now. Finally, without a strong civilian high-tech ecosystem, Russia could find itself far behind the United States and China in technological prowess. For over two decades, Russia’s leadership has been tightening its grip on the private sector. Its highly centralized decision-making has helped the Kremlin mobilize resources quickly and head off political and social developments that threaten the state, but it has also suffocated the entrepreneurial energy the country needs to regain its technological edge and compete in the marketplace of tomorrow. Russia’s innovation infrastructure remains rooted in the twentieth-century Soviet state-centered model. But today’s technological transformations—AI and robotics, clean energy, quantum computing, gene editing—demand new modes of interaction between states and private businesses, from global platforms down to the garage startups that often lead in key breakthroughs. BEYOND THE FORTRESS How Russia fares over the long run will depend on its ability to hedge against and prepare for another change in the world order. Its current “besieged fortress” model treats the international environment as a challenge rather than an opportunity. It can minimize immediate external risks, but it also keeps Russia from making full use of its geography, resources, and human capital. Perpetual confrontation with the United States and Europe does not serve Russia’s long-term development. The West may keep declining in power, but it will remain indispensable to Russia’s external environment—sometimes a problem for Moscow, sometimes part of the solution. Peaceful coexistence, and even limited cooperation, is the better path. Restoring ties with the EU matters most of all. These days, it is easy to forget that its member states were once Moscow’s main economic partners and its chief source of new technology and modern business practices. Given the dismal state of Russian-European relations, even a partial rapprochement will take considerable time. Once the conflict in Ukraine ends, however, the two sides could begin the slow work of repair. It is also in Russia’s own interest to do its part to uphold international legal norms, especially those coming from the United Nations and other global bodies, even when that means making concessions and giving up potential short-term gains. To be sure, a world governed by “might makes right” offers Moscow real opportunities in the short run. But over the long run, it is a dangerous game. The international balance of power is swiftly shifting, and new actors are rising. A strong international legal system—backed by all major powers, including Russia—may prove one of the few safeguards against revisionist temptations. Russia is, to the dismay of its critics, holding strong and proving itself in the current moment. But to sustain that success, it will have to look beyond short-term gains and narrow self-interest. It must be able to withstand upheaval in the international system and rapid technological change. Russia has the resources and wherewithal to determine its own course, but it is clinging too tightly to its preference for stability over change. This is understandable, given the painful memories of the 1990s, when change came as catastrophe, costing millions of Russians not just their jobs and savings but self-respect, belonging, even a reason to live. But that preference can also harden into a refusal to adapt—a calcification that has pushed great powers to the sidelines before. item.title: The Future of Ukraine’s Drone Democracy
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.45
On August 19, the Ukrainian parliament voted overwhelmingly to confirm Ukraine’s new defense minister, ending weeks of uncertainty at a crucial phase of the war. For more than a month, Ukrainians had taken to the streets of Kyiv and other cities to protest President Volodymyr Zelensky’s firing of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. His successor, Yevhenii Khmara, is a special operations officer, best known for leading Operation Spider’s Web, the successful attack on Russian strategic bombers deep inside Russia. But the political fallout from this summer’s upheaval is not over. The removal of Fedorov, whom many Ukrainians considered highly effective, set off a series of decisions by Zelensky to reshuffle the cabinet, and more consequentially, the heads of military and law enforcement agencies. Shortly after dismissing his defense minister, Zelensky sought to quell the public backlash by also firing Oleksandr Syrsky, the unpopular commander of the armed forces. As a result, the president was simultaneously replacing the two figures—the defense minister and the head of the military—officially responsible for Ukraine’s defense against Russia. That this was happening at the very moment Ukraine was gaining the advantage on the battlefield has made the changes all the more fraught. For one thing, the large-scale protests themselves mark a new stage in Zelensky’s relationship to the electorate. Unlike any previous protests since the full-scale invasion, Ukrainians directly challenged the president’s handling of the war, introducing a dynamic that is unlikely to go away. Perhaps even more consequential, on the eve of the parliament’s vote on Fedorov’s successor, Fedorov released a controversial video address in which he declared that Ukraine needed a “system reboot” and called for wartime elections—the first time that not merely a prominent Ukrainian figure but a member of Zelensky’s inner circle and one of his former closest allies had done so. Until now, most Ukrainians have dismissed the prospect, since elections cannot be held while the country is under martial law. Amid these developments, something else has become increasingly clear: one of the unforeseen consequences of Ukraine’s transition to drone-centered warfare has been the expansion of civil society in new ways. The embrace of a decentralized, technology-driven defense strategy has required new forms of cooperation between military and civilians, giving far more people a stake in matters of national security and military strategy. And that has created a new reality for the country’s leadership. A DIFFERENT WAR A crucial factor driving the events of this summer is the evolution of the military confrontation with Russia into a drone war. This reality, which began to take hold in 2024, has accelerated Ukraine’s transition from foreign-supplied to domestically produced weapons: some 95 percent of drones are now assembled inside the country. Moreover, although Ukraine remains heavily reliant on its scarce supply of American interceptors to defend against ballistic missile attacks, it is far less dependent on foreign systems and intelligence than it was at the start of the war. The shift to a drone-centered battle space has fundamentally altered combat tactics, the expertise required of soldiers, and the way arms are purchased. It has also rendered some kinds of legacy systems, such as armored vehicles and short-range artillery, increasingly obsolete. Yet it is not the drones themselves that have made the shift so dramatic. To exploit the full potential of unmanned warfare, Ukraine has adopted an integrated digital architecture linking unmanned platforms with situational inputs and intelligence. It has also pursued an unprecedented level of digital coordination, as well as decentralized production and procurement of weapons and of digital technologies themselves. Fedorov was one of the key architects behind the deployment of this drone infrastructure. Unlike many other officials or military leaders, he not only possessed an acute understanding of the battlefield, the weapons deployed in it, and the data streaming from it, but he also had the ability to build, coordinate, and continually upgrade a comprehensive digital system to manage it. Although he served as defense minister for only six months, Fedorov had driven this shift as the head of the Ministry of Digital Transformation, a government agency he created in 2019 and ran until 2026. Drawing on a team of specialists, the agency had set out to replace traditional bureaucratic procedures across government with more efficient digital platforms; a secondary goal was reducing corruption. After Russia’s full-scale invasion, Fedorov’s team became a driving force within the government for Ukraine’s drone program. Since the acquisition of drones initially fell outside formal procurement, the agency was able to largely run the process through its own “Drone Line” initiative. At the same time, it began building a new digital infrastructure to manage drone warfare. Some of these capabilities, such as Delta—a cloud-based system for managing the entire battlefield—had been designed earlier by volunteer-led civic initiatives. But the Ministry of Digital Transformation gave them crucial government support. It also introduced rewards for army units that successfully deployed drones and, later, for those operating unmanned maritime systems and ground robots, as well. Some military analysts worry that these kinds of incentives risk “gamifying” the war or that they oversimplify operational realities. Yet by providing continuous feedback, the programs provide valuable real-time battlefield intelligence, as well as sophisticated data sets for assessing the performance of weapons and units. Fedorov’s team, relying for a time on Zelensky’s backing, pushed for new policies and funding mechanisms to accelerate the military’s digital transformation. It also set out to streamline the military bureaucracy and bring greater transparency to wartime procurement, which has been highly vulnerable to corruption. Over 900 Ukrainian companies now produce thousands of drone models and components. To manage this huge and fragmented sector, the ministry introduced new systems to coordinate logistics, certification, and deployment. Overall, these changes have been significant. Step by step, drones have allowed Ukraine’s armed forces to acquire or sustain capabilities that have traditionally come from missiles and airpower. In 2025, Ukraine had reached parity in the air domain with Russia along the frontline; by 2026, Ukrainian drones and missiles were also able to reach Russian command-and-control centers, cut off logistics, and prevent some Russian assaults. Although Moscow can still outcompete on resources, using oil revenues and vast state spending to finance its aggression, Ukraine’s new digital architecture has enabled it to do more with less, multiplying the effect of particular weapons by connecting sensors, operators, and strike platforms into a unified system. NEW WEAPONS, OLD WAYS Despite their undeniable value, these innovations have often come from outside Ukraine’s military establishment, and sometimes in opposition to it. Overshadowed by the large number of civilian recruits after 2022 is the fact that the Ukrainian army began the war staffed by professional soldiers, with inherited doctrines and lines of command. Although the military established the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch in 2024, its traditional mechanized, infantry, and armored brigades still bore the brunt of the fighting while integrating drones at their own pace. And as with any large national armed forces, the existing hierarchy has resisted wholesale change. Many commanders have embraced drones as weapons—just as they would tanks or guns—yet without fully understanding the structural changes needed to make them effective. Similarly, Ukraine’s established defense industry, which has long counted on existing relationships and contracts, has also resisted the overhaul. Until recently, drone contracting has remained a comparatively small sector. Even though it involves hundreds of millions of dollars, expensive traditional capabilities such as artillery and other conventional weapons systems continue to consume most of Ukraine’s defense budget. Over the past year, however, the balance has shifted: the military’s procurement priorities and the financial interests surrounding them have begun to adjust to drone-centered warfare. And that has created new forms of pushback. Almost from the beginning of his tenure as defense minister, Fedorov and his team were targeted by smear campaigns on anonymous Telegram channels. These have linked him to various military scandals and alleged corruption in the drone industry. Fedorov blames the attacks on entrenched interests—defense contractors and powerful insiders—who were threatened by the shift in war priorities. As one example, he has cited his successful efforts to reduce the price of a procurement deal for short-range artillery that was becoming obsolete, given the expanding kill zones. He also said that Zelensky had received persistent complaints that the digital reformers were breaking a functioning system and disrupting the delivery of essential equipment to frontline troops. At the same time, as large amounts of funding, especially from Ukraine’s international partners, have been directed at drone technology, established defense contractors and well-connected political actors have sought to gain a piece of the pie. They are now moving aggressively to compete with drone startups on drone contracts. Taken together, these tensions brought pressure on Zelensky to move more slowly on the military transformation—which Fedorov had been pushing to accelerate. But the president had failed to understand just how much the public had become invested in Ukraine’s new way of war, and the remarkable results it had begun to achieve. PRESSURE FROM BELOW By the spring of 2026, if defense contractors had misgivings about Fedorov, the Ukrainian public had become increasingly dissatisfied with Syrsky, Ukraine’s commander in chief. Syrsky had notched several strategic victories, including the battle for Kyiv and the liberation of the Kharkiv region during the first year of the all-out war. He had also embraced drone warfare, expanding drone procurement and battlefield integration, although that was part of the army’s broader evolution. Yet many soldiers saw him as a commander who emphasized discipline and was prepared to sacrifice lives when he considered it necessary to achieve a military objective. Within the military, Syrsky had long taken pride in staying close to the frontlines, sometimes to the point of micromanaging the battlefield. But there was also a growing sense among officers and soldiers that he was beginning to value personal loyalty within the command structure above military effectiveness. He had a tendency to sideline talented younger officers and to use his control over promotions and resources to consolidate his own influence. According to some soldiers and officers, these habits risked undermining battlefield readiness, including on the most critical sectors of the front. Then, in June, Ukrainian journalists published a bombshell investigation uncovering horrific allegations of abuse in an assault regiment—a unit that had been given privileged support by Syrsky. The revelations included evidence of violence and unlawful killings within the unit. Although a formal military investigation followed, public criticism remained intense and serving military personnel spoke out. Many laid the blame on Syrsky personally for allowing this to happen. It was after this scandal that Zelensky made the ill-timed decision to fire Fedorov. In the eyes of many Ukrainians, the president was siding with those who opposed reforms. Almost immediately, thousands of people took to the streets of Kyiv and other cities. To contain the public outcry, Zelensky then moved quickly to fire Syrsky and install Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi as his replacement, a choice that was broadly welcomed. Drapatyi, 43, had entered the military in 2014 as a battalion commander and risen through the ranks, while taking part in many defining battles. He is known for embracing new approaches, including the digital battlefield promoted by Fedorov, supporting promising officers, challenging army leaders when necessary, and championing operations that minimize casualties—a priority that Ukrainians value. Meanwhile, Zelensky named Khmara to replace Fedorov. Since 2011, Khmara—in his late 30s or early 40s—had served in Alpha, the Security Service of Ukraine’s special forces unit, and was considered to have an unblemished record. (He had to leave active military service and formally become a civilian before assuming the post, which by law must be held by a civilian.) Yet Zelensky’s moves failed to resolve the underlying tension between the Defense Ministry and the military’s general staff. By law, the defense minister is supposed to nominate the commander in chief to the president. But this time, Zelensky once again effectively selected the commander himself, creating a situation in which the general staff continues to see that it answers to the president, not to the defense minister. LOST MOMENTUM? A larger question is how this political upheaval will affect the war. Fedorov was fired just as the reforms he had been advocating for were helping Ukraine turn the tide against Russia. By spring 2026, Ukrainian long-range drone strikes were beginning to erode one of Russia’s greatest strategic advantages: its oil sector. Kyiv also continued to disrupt Russian logistics in the south, particularly in Crimea, while also attacking oil refineries across the European part of Russia, including Moscow and St. Petersburg. But many wonder whether Fedorov’s dismissal will slow that progress. In Russia, pro-war commentators openly celebrated Zelensky’s decision, viewing it as a rejection of one of the main architects of Ukraine’s military modernization. Hours after his dismissal, representatives of several foreign governments and international technology firms, including the Italian minister of defense and Palantir’s CEO, Alex Karp, offered him positions, which he declined. Zelensky has also offered him several alternative roles in Kyiv, but Fedorov has refused them all because they came with limited decision-making power. Still, he seems almost certain to gain an important place within the government or defense sector sooner or later. Despite Zelensky’s appointment of innovation-minded leaders to replace Fedorov and Syrsky, the future of Ukraine’s digital war ecosystem remains uncertain. Unlike Khmara, who takes office without an established cadre, Fedorov brought to the defense ministry the team he had already built at the Ministry of Digital Transformation. Although only a few of the digitization specialists Fedorov brought to the Defense Ministry have left so far, many more may be pushed out. By calling for elections, Fedorov signaled a move into opposition, raising questions about whether his relationship with Zelensky would deteriorate—and what this would mean for close associates still holding official posts. By design, Ukraine’s digital battlefield infrastructure has the capacity to rapidly evolve in response to changing combat demands. The system can function without Fedorov or his team, but it remains unclear whether it can maintain the pace of evolution needed to stay ahead of Russia. The immediate risk is lost momentum. DEMOCRACY IN THE BALANCE The democratic culture that took hold in Ukraine in 2014 and drove the protests this summer continues to be one of the country’s greatest military strengths. Many of Ukraine’s most important military adaptations have come from below—from individual soldiers and commanders but also from civilian entrepreneurs. Hundreds of private initiatives have advanced technologies, software, manufacturing, and logistics in ways that have dramatically improved the way Ukraine fights. Too many military units, entrepreneurs, engineers, and civic activists are now invested in this ecosystem for a single political decision to dismantle it. But the disruption could affect Ukraine’s ability to iterate new advances on the battlefield—at a moment when the overall dynamic of the war hangs in the balance. For Zelensky, the political damage of his decisions this summer cannot be undone. Ukrainians have largely remained united behind the president in the face of external pressure, including after Donald Trump’s return to the White House in 2025. Nonetheless, he has shown more than once that he is out of step with ordinary Ukrainians. Already a year ago, his effort to restrict the role of Ukraine’s anticorruption authorities provoked major protests and significantly diminished confidence in his leadership. Now, his decision to fire Fedorov has only reinforced that perception. Until this summer, Fedorov had avoided attention, presenting himself as a manager, not a politician. Yet Zelensky’s abrupt decision to dismiss him—for reasons the public still does not understand—made Fedorov one of Ukraine’s most popular figures almost overnight. Now, Fedorov’s call for elections has significantly raised the stakes. In his video address, Fedorov—without mentioning names—again spoke about powerful vested interests that have meddled in government and defense and resisted the changes Ukraine needs to maintain its military advantage. He also asserted that, with no end to the war in sight, Ukraine needs a broader debate about political accountability and decision-making. Clarifying his initially vague but surprising address, the former minister pledged to outline the technical and security logistics of wartime voting—specifically for soldiers, refugees, and frontline residents—to enable a realistic debate on holding elections. Under martial law, elections are barred. Until now, only external powers—Russia or the United States—had questioned Ukraine’s political legitimacy without elections. Most Ukrainians deemed wartime voting dangerous and impractical, fearing that staging elections would simply divert attention, funds, and effort from the front. But Zelensky is in his seventh year as president, under a constitution that permits two consecutive five-year terms. Having made consequential, unpopular decisions, he has increasingly given the sense that he has stopped reading the country’s mood. Fedorov’s announcement may not precipitate an immediate change, but it has started a debate that could play out in the coming months and years. Until now, when it came to the question of holding elections, it had seemed that Ukraine would know when the moment arrived: at some point, in an active, outspoken society, even during war, Ukrainians themselves would demand democratic accountability. This does not mean that Fedorov will automatically gain popularity if he decides to run. His call for wartime voting has alienated some public figures and politicians who backed him as defense minister. They see his intervention now as less a push for accountability than an open political challenge to Zelensky—one that risks draining attention from the reforms that Fedorov had previously championed. With the war likely to continue for the foreseeable future, the urgent question facing the country now is to what degree the people should be given a direct say in the war’s course: how it fights, by what means, according to what strategy, and with what broader vision for its defense. The rise of drone warfare has made military strategy more inclusive, giving a wider range of people—from civil society representatives and tech innovators to members of frontline military units—the expertise and leverage to shape it. That means, on a popular level, more engagement in the war than ever. But for the country’s leaders, it has also created a powerful new set of voices to be reckoned with and be held accountable to—ones that, in the future, may well demand an even greater say.
