item.title: How al-Qaeda Ended
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.37
Al-Qaeda has ended. The organization that Osama bin Laden founded and led, that attacked the United States 25 years ago and killed 2,977 innocent Americans in the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and rural Pennsylvania, no longer survives—and U.S. officials should say so, instead of burnishing the group’s legacy by acting and speaking as if it still exists. Terrorism has not ceased, jihadism has not gone away, and the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran may ignite more anti-American sentiment and violence. But the group that attacked the United States on 9/11 is finished. In the years following that assault, thousands of Americans dedicated their lives to avenging the victims. The nationwide horror of watching planes go into towers—innocent people crushed, burned, or jumping to their deaths—catalyzed a passionate response. And the cost to those who responded was high: in the post-9/11 wars, more than 15,000 U.S. military members and contractors died in combat, and some 1.8 million became disabled. And from 2012 to 2021, four times as many active-duty or veteran military members died by suicide as died in combat. Service members from loyal U.S. allies, especially Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom, joined the United States in combat; hundreds of them died fighting alongside Americans. They and their families deserve to know their efforts were not in vain. Washington and its allies lost the war in Afghanistan but succeeded against al-Qaeda. Jihadist terrorism persists as a threat, and not every group using the name “al-Qaeda” has been neutralized. Dangerous organizations operate in the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa, North Africa, the Sahel, and South Asia. They carry out attacks and hold territory, and some have come close to taking down governments, especially in Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. Jihadists of various stripes train in Taliban-governed Afghanistan—a development that must be closely monitored. But none of what are sometimes called “al-Qaeda affiliates” is centrally directed or led by bin Laden’s organization, and officials should cease suggesting they are, since doing so inflates the threat they pose without making it any easier to combat them. Indeed, it would be best to cease using the term “al-Qaeda affiliate” altogether. Studying the pattern of attacks tied directly to al-Qaeda shows how the central organization ran out of steam. Before 9/11, the core al-Qaeda organization kept up a steady pace of global operations against U.S. targets, with a track record that included the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Center (six dead, more than 1,000 injured), the 1996 bombing of Khobar Towers (19 killed, hundreds injured), the 1998 bombing of the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (224 killed, thousands injured), and the 2000 attack on the USS Cole (17 killed). After 2001, core al-Qaeda’s efforts against the U.S. homeland included a fumbled 2001 attempt to ignite a bomb placed in a shoe on an airliner bound for Miami and a failed 2009 suicide bombing plot targeting the New York City subway. The group caused more pain for U.S. friends and allies than for the United States itself, with deadly attacks in Bali in 2002, Riyadh in 2003, and London in 2005. But following that spike in the first decade of the twenty-first century, the momentum shifted to other jihadist groups, and after 2009, core al-Qaeda’s global operations essentially ceased. For decades, I have studied how terrorist groups end, based on a dataset of 457 terrorist campaigns and organizations going back a century. By analyzing their makeup, targets, and intended audiences, one can identify common trajectories. Although not mutually exclusive, there are six major pathways such groups ultimately take: decapitation, negotiation, success, failure, repression, and reorientation to another mode of operation (such as ordinary criminality or insurgency). In the case of core al-Qaeda, although decapitation and military repression played important roles, the group ended primarily through strategic failure—just as bin Laden feared it would. A MOVING TARGET In the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks, the U.S. campaign should have been focused on destroying the perpetrators. But the United States failed to clearly define the threat. The Authorization for the Use of Military Force that Congress passed on September 14, 2001, did not mention al-Qaeda at all, instead vaguely identifying Washington’s enemies as “those nations, organizations or persons [the president] determines planned, authorized, committed or aided the terrorist attacks that occurred on September 11, 2001.” A few days later, President George W. Bush echoed that framing. “Our war on al-Qaeda begins with al-Qaeda but it does not end there,” he declared. “It will not end until every terrorist group of global reach has been found, stopped, and defeated.” With that, the United States declared war on a tactic, one that had shaped political violence in the modern world since anarchist terrorism swept through Europe before World War I. Washington had set itself a task it could never accomplish. Making the enemy “terrorism” meant its efforts would lack clarity and drag on endlessly. What followed was an ill-focused campaign in Afghanistan (which removed the Taliban from power in Kabul but allowed bin Laden and his cronies to escape) and then the war in Iraq, where al-Qaeda had not even operated until an affiliate emerged after the U.S. military occupation had been in place for a year. The invasion of Iraq did more to prolong the life of al-Qaeda than any other single event, drawing fresh recruits from Sunni populations all over the world, and eventually creating the conditions for the emergence of the Islamic State organization. Still, in the 25 years that followed, sometimes almost despite itself, the United States along with its allies did defeat bin Laden’s al-Qaeda—often with inadvertent help from the group itself. An important factor was the May 2011 killing of Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan, an event that undermined al-Qaeda’s coherence. U.S. forces stormed bin Laden’s compound, killed him, and then helicoptered his body to an aircraft carrier and buried it at sea, leaving no possibility for a memorial or focal point for his followers. The documents recovered in that raid were just as valuable to U.S. counterterrorism as bin Laden’s death, offering compelling evidence that he had not been centrally directing the group’s operations for some time. His death did not end al-Qaeda, but it was justice served, and it undercut the ability of his fans to rally around him. By September 2011, U.S. officials were claiming that the number of surviving people directly connected to carrying out the 9/11 attacks was no more than a couple of dozen. But instead of declaring victory over the group at that point and moving on, the U.S. drone campaign, which had begun in 2002 under Bush and accelerated in the early Obama administration, expanded its scope and target set. Instead of so-called personality attacks (which target known leaders), the campaign shifted to “signature strikes,” targeting unidentified individuals or groups who fit a particular profile, not just in Afghanistan and Pakistan but also in Somalia and Yemen. The drone campaign degraded al-Qaeda’s ranks and avenged attempted attacks—for example, by eliminating members of al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate who trained and equipped Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab, the would-be “underwear bomber” who tried to bring down a civilian airliner in 2009. But drone attacks also catalyzed terrorism: according to declassified FBI interviews, the 2013 Boston Marathon bomber, Tamerlan Tsarnaev (likewise inspired by al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate), told a friend that his killing of an eight-year-old in that attack was justified because children in Afghanistan and Pakistan had been killed by U.S. drones. The drone campaign had a strategic impact on U.S. allies: public attitudes in France, Germany, Spain, Turkey, and the United Kingdom hardened against Washington’s “global war on terrorism.” Drones were tactically important and probably saved lives, but they did not end al-Qaeda. More critical to that success was intelligence and law-enforcement collaboration among U.S. allies, which remains the bedrock of American counterterrorism. New measures to curb terrorist financing, biometric screening and databases, and new ways of sharing intelligence among allies helped Washington monitor threats beyond American shores. In 2006, for example, close cooperation between U.S. and British intelligence services thwarted an al-Qaeda-linked plot to smuggle the explosive TATP in beverage containers and take down U.S.-bound civilian aircraft over the Atlantic. THINGS FALL APART But much of the damage al-Qaeda suffered was self-inflicted. A key driver was a backlash against terrorist attacks that hurt Muslim civilians and a resulting loss of support among communities al-Qaeda supposedly represented. Bin Laden knew this was a weakness, and his frustration shows in the communications discovered in the Abbottabad compound. A May 2010 letter he wrote to one of his deputies warns, “This is when we lose the perception of the Muslims towards us, which is that we are the ones defending the Muslims and fighting their biggest enemy, the Crusader Zionist alliance…[and instead] killing those that the general public consider Muslims.” Al-Qaeda started building global franchises in 2004, but they typically emerged out of existing organizations, and their operational ties to core al-Qaeda could be hazy. According to bin Laden’s own assessment, rogue affiliates hurt al-Qaeda’s cause more than they helped it, since most victims of their violence were Muslim civilians, whose families and communities then blamed al-Qaeda. According to the Pew Global Attitudes project, between 2003 and 2011, support for bin Laden personally had dropped in Indonesia from 59 percent to 26 percent, in Jordan from 56 percent to 13 percent, and in the Palestinian territories from 72 percent to 34 percent. In Pakistan, where bin Laden was hiding, support for him plunged from 46 percent in 2003 to 18 percent in 2010. A decade after 9/11, bin Laden’s dream of a vanguard uniting Muslims had evaporated. Internal divisions also played a role in al-Qaeda’s demise. The most dramatic split was with the Islamic State, or ISIS, which had started out as an al-Qaeda affiliate before rebranding. In 2014, ISIS conquered major parts of Iraq and Syria, drawing some 15,000 foreign fighters from 80 countries to join its self-declared caliphate. This was a huge challenge to the original group: al-Qaeda had ideas, but ISIS had territory. ISIS’s trajectory reflected the core problem of dealing with affiliates who did not share (or necessarily even grasp) bin Laden’s strategy. In 2005, bin Laden’s chief deputy, Ayman al-Zawahiri, wrote to Abu Musab al-Zarqawi—the leader of what was then known as al-Qaeda in Iraq and would eventually become ISIS—advising him to stop killing Shiite civilians and beheading hostages in grotesque videos. “Among the things which the feelings of the Muslim populace who love and support you will never find palatable … are the scenes of slaughtering the hostages,” Zawahiri wrote. “We don’t need this.” Zarqawi ignored him. In 2006, a U.S. airstrike killed Zarqawi. But for the next decade, global jihadism shifted firmly in his direction, and against the comparatively more cautious approach of al-Qaeda. Much of the damage al-Qaeda suffered was self-inflicted. Even as ISIS swamped al-Qaeda, however, the limits of its approach became clear, vindicating Zawahiri’s warning. The first mistake ISIS made was to gather forces and materiel in a concentrated space, becoming a perfect target for conventional military force. Its second error was to enthusiastically embrace gruesome forms of brutality and sadism, antagonizing virtually everyone who did not belong to the group; by 2016, almost the entire world had united against it. Working with Iraqi, Kurdish, and Syrian forces, a global coalition to defeat ISIS had by 2019 recaptured the territory the group had seized and destroyed the caliphate. But for al-Qaeda, the damage had been done: it had lost its foothold in Iraq and split its recruitment base with a younger, flashier brand. Zawahiri’s response was to decentralize and focus on groups in South Asia and North Africa, such as al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent and al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, which primarily sought to overthrow local governments. In July 2022, nearly a year after the American withdrawal from Afghanistan, a U.S. drone strike in Kabul killed Zawahiri. The muted response to his death confirmed the weakness of core al-Qaeda. Today, the apparent head of al-Qaeda is Said al-Adel, who lives in Iran, a Shiite-majority country where, for a decade after 9/11, he and other al-Qaeda leaders and their families spent years living under a form of house arrest, and where his room to maneuver remains strictly limited. He has not even declared himself the group’s leader, perhaps because he fears assassination—but perhaps because there is, in reality, nothing for him to lead. Although the group could one day reinvent itself or carry out attacks sponsored or abetted by Iran, the al-Qaeda that attacked the United States 25 years ago has ended. The United States sometimes accelerated and sometimes slowed the group’s demise. But ultimately, al-Qaeda failed. item.title: America Doesn’t Need More Nuclear Weapons
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.31
How many nuclear weapons is enough? The question has haunted policymakers and scholars for 80 years. Early in the Cold War, the United States expanded its nuclear arsenal rapidly in response to the Soviet threat. But beginning in the 1980s, as the two nuclear powers sought ways to reduce nuclear risks, arms treaties helped cut the size of those arsenals significantly, and stockpiles decreased by 80 percent. Now, circumstances are pushing the United States to consider the size of its nuclear arsenal once again. Over the past six years, China has nearly tripled the number of nuclear weapons it has, and according to the U.S. Defense Department, the country is on track to have over 1,000 by 2030. China is not yet a nuclear peer to Russia and the United States, which each deploy roughly 1,550 nuclear weapons in keeping with the limit set by the 2010 New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, but parity may be Beijing’s goal. Meanwhile, the last formal barrier to a U.S.-Russian arms race fell away when New START expired earlier this year. Faced with these rising dangers, the Trump administration announced in March that it would conduct what it called a “nuclear strategy review.” Some strategists recommend that the review include a call for a larger and more diverse nuclear arsenal. A larger arsenal, proponents of expansion argue, would provide the United States with a wider array of choices, especially for an in-kind response to low-yield theater nuclear attacks. Although Russia and the United States have nearly the same number of weapons, Russia possesses a greater number of theater nuclear weapons, which, unlike strategic nuclear forces, are designed for tactical use on the battlefield. China may also be developing more of these types of weapons. Advocates of expansion propose that if Washington can match any nuclear attack blow for blow, Beijing and Moscow will be less likely to initiate a nuclear exchange. According to Trump administration officials, the nuclear review will look at this “theater nuclear forces issue” to “identify where there may need to be changes or additions made.” The United States should take additions to its nuclear forces off the table. The country already has a vast and diverse enough supply of nuclear weapons to unleash devastation on an adversary in the case of a nuclear attack. The purpose of nuclear deterrence is not to have an answer for every weapon in an adversary’s arsenal, but to avoid crossing the nuclear threshold in the first place. Moreover, introducing new theater weapons could provoke an arms race for which the United States is ill equipped and invite risks of inadvertent escalation that would only make the country more vulnerable. Rather than focus on expanding and diversifying the U.S. nuclear arsenal, Washington’s deterrence strategy should attend to the modernization of its existing strategic forces, which is behind schedule, and of its conventional arms, which are not fit to deter the United States’ greatest military threats, especially Chinese military aggression in the Western Pacific. MAXED OUT When the foundations of U.S. nuclear doctrine were laid early in the Cold War, escalation was understood as a ladder. When states encountered crises, their retaliatory actions would follow a vertical climb to more dangerous “rungs.” But escalation is unlikely to follow such a neat path, as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby argued in May; instead, as he said, there are ways that nuclear powers can shape “the limits of a conflict” and influence how their opponents respond. The goal for modern U.S. nuclear doctrine, therefore, should not be an abstract conception of superiority at all levels of the escalation ladder but practical options to constrain and deter the adversary. The proposal to introduce new theater nuclear forces in Asia or Europe follows the outdated logic that escalation will progress in a rational, orderly way with increasing levels of violence and harm. It does not follow modern reality. Without arms controls in place, Washington does need to modernize its strategic nuclear forces—high-yield weapons whose purpose is to hold valuable targets at risk—to deter and defend against a nuclear attack on the American homeland or on U.S. allies’ territory. It has been trying to do so for years, since the U.S. Senate ratified New START in 2010, but with mixed results. As part of a deal to gain Senate support for the treaty, U.S. President Barack Obama approved a multidecade program to upgrade the existing nuclear arsenal and delivery systems that is now costing at least $1 trillion. The decision paved the way for defense contractors and national laboratories to begin replacing bombers, ground-based intercontinental ballistic missiles, submarines, warheads, and military communications systems. More than 15 years later, most of the United States’ nuclear modernization efforts are over budget and behind schedule, despite significant investments in workforce, infrastructure, and congressional appropriations that fulfill and sometimes exceed the funding the Pentagon has requested. In 2015, for example, Congress required that 80 plutonium components for nuclear weapons be built by 2030; Department of Energy officials have since deemed the task impossible. The Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile program was at least 81 percent over budget in 2024, and its first flight test has been delayed by about four years. The B-21 bomber program, which is on track, is the exception, not the rule. The United States is now at risk of nuclear disarmament by default. When the current systems reach end of life, replacements may not be ready. New work orders to build new weapons would only further stretch the nuclear enterprise’s capacity. CROSSING THE RUBICON Expanding the U.S. arsenal would not only distract from modernization efforts. It would also invite new risks. A U.S. buildup would likely trigger a steady arms race with other nuclear states—the very outcome that Democratic and Republican administrations worked for decades to avoid through negotiations and mutual arms reduction agreements with Russia. And given the slow pace of the current nuclear modernization drive and the heavy burdens already falling on the U.S. defense industrial base, the United States today is not well positioned to win such a race. The danger would not stop there. The greater the number and diversity of nuclear weapons, the greater the number of possible miscalculations and signaling problems in a crisis. For example, it would be difficult to distinguish between a nuclear-armed cruise missile that is launched from a fighter jet or submarine and a conventional missile. If the United States builds these capabilities, the Chinese and Russian militaries could mistakenly believe that an incoming conventional U.S. munition is nuclear. And because of the uncertainty, the risk of nuclear use would rise exponentially. As long as no U.S. leader wants to fight a nuclear war, additional nuclear options, including more low-yield weapons, will be extraneous. Nuclear weapons are not effective for coercing an adversary during a conflict. If Washington responded to a nuclear attack with a nuclear weapon, whether that weapon was of similar yield or caused comparable damage, its opponent would not likely back down. Damage assessments would be hazy. Leaders would be likely to take on more, not less, risk, becoming more inclined to widen the war and respond with more nuclear attacks, including on U.S. territory. Deterrence requires that an adversary perceive both that a U.S. leader will use force and that an alternative course of action is preferable. A more diverse U.S. nuclear arsenal complicates any attempts to reassure the adversary that there is a better way out of a crisis. Ultimately, the potential benefits of expanding the U.S. nuclear arsenal do not justify the costs. This is not to discount the rising nuclear threats from China and Russia. In 2018, Russian President Vladimir Putin announced that Russia would test dangerous new nuclear delivery systems that can loiter near the U.S. coast or maneuver at hypersonic speeds. China has built new silos in its western desert and has tested ballistic missiles in the Pacific. Neither U.S. nuclear weapons nor U.S. missile defense systems such as Golden Dome are likely to eliminate novel Russian systems or China’s nuclear expansion. Still, the United States’ 1,550 deployed bombs and warheads deter nuclear attacks from both China and Russia, provide counterstrike options to limit damage to the homeland if nuclear war does occur, and fulfill U.S. security commitments to allies and partners. Once China has nearly as many nuclear weapons as Russia and the United States, Washington may have new opportunities to pursue new arms control agreements with Beijing and Moscow. THE NONNUCLEAR OPTION The United States has long had good reason to place limits on its nuclear forces. In 1964, Defense Secretary Robert McNamara made the point that nuclear bombs would have diminishing returns once 400 strategic warheads—far fewer than Washington had at the time or has today—struck Soviet cities. Arms control agreements between Moscow and Washington since the 1970s have allowed the United States to avoid costly arms races. Dedicating funds to defense research and development enabled the U.S. military to achieve comparative advantages in conventional warfare capabilities, including advanced reconnaissance, combined arms, and precision strikes. Innovative conventional weapons still deliver options for U.S. presidents. The Trump administration should similarly be thinking about nuclear weapons in the context of the United States’ broader military and deterrence strategy. Nuclear posture reviews have consistently affirmed, over the last four decades, that weapons in the U.S. arsenal are defensive, meant to deter aggression, and defeat peer adversaries if deterrence fails. In practice, the primary means of demonstrating the United States’ resolve to deny and defeat its rivals is conventional. The U.S. bombing of Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and Ukrainian drone strikes on military and industrial facilities deep within Russia over the last two years were conventional operations that achieved their tactical objectives. It would be sensible practice to include nuclear reviews as part of the national defense strategy process, as the last U.S. administration did. Isolating nuclear strategy from conventional force decisions is a mistake. To be sure, conventional forces are not a substitute for nuclear weapons. But to credibly deter China and Russia, the United States needs nonnuclear options. The Trump administration has weakened U.S. conventional deterrence over the past year by pausing arms sales to Taiwan, shifting munitions to the Middle East, and beginning to withdraw American troops from Germany. Those steps must be reversed, and Washington must increase production of conventional forces capable of facing persistent threats in Asia and Europe, which includes both exquisite, or expensive and technologically advanced forces, as well as cheaper, mass-produced forces. U.S. policymakers should follow through on the promise of the third offset, an approach set out in 2014 for using unmanned and autonomous systems to counter Chinese and Russian military advances. With advanced conventional forces produced at scale, the United States can make the costs of war too high for China or Russia to initiate a conflict. It is true that the global nuclear environment is changing. The United States must meet the prospect of two nuclear peers with foresight and planning. But the solution is not simply amassing more weapons. Building a larger and more diverse nuclear arsenal would put Washington on a path to undermining, rather than strengthening, deterrence. To counter both China and Russia, the United States must focus on modernizing its existing strategic nuclear capabilities and strengthening its conventional deterrence to preclude escalation. Because once a conflict transcends the nuclear threshold, no one can win. item.title: Berlin Is Shedding Light on the Gray Zone
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.12
Berlin Is Shedding Light on the Gray Zone Are European countries finally ready to publicly call out Russian sabotage? Identifying state sponsors of gray-zone acts is extremely difficult—by design. But if a targeted country manages to identify the state sponsor of an attack against it, should it make its identity known? Earlier this month, Germany announced that Russia was behind the incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in which a suspicious drone was identified, thankfully before it could do damage. Berlin’s announcement was a brave decision, because attribution, particularly involving bellicose nations such as Russia, brings the risk of escalation. But with gray-zone acts proliferating in number and variety, this is a decision any targeted country should be ready to make. On Sept. 1, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul walked up to a podium in Berlin in front of a crowd of journalists. Identifying state sponsors of gray-zone acts is extremely difficult—by design. But if a targeted country manages to identify the state sponsor of an attack against it, should it make its identity known? Earlier this month, Germany announced that Russia was behind the incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in which a suspicious drone was identified, thankfully before it could do damage. Berlin’s announcement was a brave decision, because attribution, particularly involving bellicose nations such as Russia, brings the risk of escalation. But with gray-zone acts proliferating in number and variety, this is a decision any targeted country should be ready to make. On Sept. 1, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul walked up to a podium in Berlin in front of a crowd of journalists. “For some time,” Dobrindt said, “our security agencies have been monitoring a high level of threat posed by hybrid activities in Germany and across Europe. These actions target critical infrastructure, defense companies, and support efforts for Ukraine. Intelligence gathered by our own services and partner agencies points clearly to Russian involvement in these hybrid operations—whether planned, executed, or thwarted.” Dobrindt continued: “Regarding the attempted attack at Leipzig airport on Aug. 4, we have the following information: The means employed—including the drone configuration, various components, and the explosive and ignition technology—are consistent with those known to us from other hybrid operations conducted by Russia and from its war against Ukraine. The technology found at the scene and the integration of the individual elements demonstrate a professional level of sophistication, revealing significant technical expertise and substantial organizational effort in both the planning and execution of the act. The actual carrying out of the attempted attack is attributable to low-level operatives.” The interior minister provided more evidence, but the news had been delivered: Russia was the instigator of the attack. “The Russian consulate-general in Bonn will be closed,” Wadephul declared, adding that the rental agreement for the Russian House in Berlin—a cultural center suspected of also serving as a hub for Russian intelligence activities—would be terminated. Ten, even five years ago, Germany and most other countries were extremely cautious in attributing gray-zone attacks to Russia or any other country. To be sure, in some cases, hostile states’ involvement was obvious: During the artificial refugee crisis that erupted on the borders of Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland in the summer of 2021, for example, Belarus didn’t even try to hide its involvement; Minsk had provided Belarusian visas for the mostly Middle Eastern nationals, then transported them to the border. But in many cases where hostile-state participation was more difficult to trace, as in case of the devastating NotPetya malware, or with the assassination attempt on former Russian intelligence officer Sergei Skripal, governments did make attributions—after having identified Russian involvement. Part of the issue is that establishing state involvement beyond reasonable doubt—the bar that democratic countries set themselves—is difficult and sometimes impossible. There’s a reason why countries such as Russia often use proxies or hire gig workers to do their dirty work. But more importantly, publicly laying blame for an attack can put countries at risk. The attacker is likely to flatly deny involvement, as Russia has with every gray-zone act attributed to it by Western governments. Worse, even as countries deny involvement, they can still retaliate for being blamed. This is, in fact, what happened after Dobrindt and Wadephul made their announcement. “Leipzig, at the airport. They found a drone there and said it was Russian. No one ever clarified the matter. Strictly speaking, that marks the beginning of a real war,” Sergey Lavrov told Russian state television. Somehow, the Russian foreign minister managed to blend evasion and denial then add a threat, all in a single statement. Germany’s response to the Leipzig incident—the closure of the consulate-general and the Russian House—is hardly provocative. If even such a moderate response prompts menacing theatrics from the Kremlin, what’s a targeted country to do? Saying nothing is certainly not an option, not anymore. With gray-zone acts, especially Russian ones, becoming more common and more brazen, the public has become aware of their existence and destructive power. If governments decided that public attributions were too dangerous and said nothing, then their citizens would call them cowardly and suspect nefarious intrigues. What’s more, Lavrov can only accuse Germany of having started “a real war” a few times. If he and others complain about supposed new wars each time that a country identifies the Kremlin as the instigator of dangerous acts, they will start looking like the schoolyard bully that only has one response in his arsenal. No—now that gray-zone acts have become part of daily life, those instigating them must be called out. And the calling out should be directed not only at the hostile state behind the deed but also directed at the public at home. By keeping the nation informed about the activities taking place in society’s midst, governments can help citizens understand the seriousness of the situation (without unduly frightening them). Public reaction, perhaps predictably, has been mixed, between those who worry that the German government is escalating and those who insist that it should not back down. In one call-in show on the WDR public radio station, a listener voiced suspicion: “Do we really believe that the Russians would attack us using two little pistols and what I would call three toy drones? They have totally different options. Our governments and other governments want this to escalate.” Another listener, though, wanted an even more forceful reaction: “What would happen if we didn’t react to these kinds of attacks?” Even without taking radical steps, Germany and other targeted countries could respond more assertively by focusing on transparency. In the Philippines, the authorities have taken to documenting every act of Chinese harassment of Philippine vessels in the South China Sea and sharing the content with the world. To be sure, documenting random acts of Russian sabotage would be harder than filming constant harassment by Chinese vessels. But whatever can be documented ought to be publicly shared. The public would, among other things, see the sorry figures who, for a small financial reward, set fire to buildings, sabotage railways, and try to wreak havoc with drones. That way, citizens would understand that while gray-zone aggression is dangerous and devious, it is also profoundly pusillanimous. item.title: Why Is China’s Officer Corps So Sprawling?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.90
Why Is China’s Officer Corps So Sprawling? Not every People’s Liberation Army general commands troops. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief. Last year, we explored what life is like for soldiers in the People’s Liberation Army. This week, in lieu of our usual news coverage, we’re turning our attention to the officer corps and what their jobs entail—especially in some of the Chinese military’s more unique roles. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief. Last year, we explored what life is like for soldiers in the People’s Liberation Army. This week, in lieu of our usual news coverage, we’re turning our attention to the officer corps and what their jobs entail—especially in some of the Chinese military’s more unique roles. What Exactly Is a PLA Officer? Chinese President Xi Jinping is married to a major general in the People’s Liberation Army (PLA)—sort of. Xi’s second wife, Peng Liyuan, is a famous singer who joined the PLA’s entertainment corps in 1980, at the age of 18. She spent her career working within the military’s vast entertainment apparatus, which performs for troops as well as operating record labels, film studios, and other commercial media businesses. Peng never commanded soldiers or wielded a weapon, yet when she was appointed head of the PLA Academy of Art in 2012, she was granted the formal military rank of major general—a title commonly given to entertainers who work for the military. Comedian Huang Hong, for instance, was also made a major general in 2012 after being hired to run the PLA’s August First Film Studio. These examples are a reminder of just how sprawling the concept of an officer can be in the world’s largest military, where they perform an array of jobs that either don’t exist in Western militaries or are usually handled by civilian contractors. China has spent decades trying to simplify the officer corps system and reduce the number of personnel with military ranks, but it is still a mess. (I won’t even get into China’s paramilitary forces.) There are two significant distinctions within the PLA officer corps: the split between command and technical staff; and the division within the command track between regular commanders and political officers, which was formalized in 2021. As in Western militaries, PLA command officers generally enter through universities or military academies, and those promoted from enlisted ranks are typically sent to military academies before advancing further. Regular commanders are responsible for battlefield command and military readiness, as in the traditional Western view of a military officer. The latter is especially important, since the PLA hasn’t fought a war since 1979. Even though their roles are not explicitly political, commanders’ careers are shaped by politics; Chinese Communist Party (CCP) membership is effectively compulsory. Political officers, sometimes called “commissars” in English, are the CCP’s eyes and ears inside the military. They monitor their regular counterparts for signs of disloyalty, run political-education programs, and watch for corruption. They are also responsible for more mundane tasks involving soldiers’ welfare, including living conditions, family visits, and career planning. The split between command and political officers dates to the Soviet Red Army and was intended to reinforce communist control of the military. Mao Zedong famously asserted that “political power comes from the barrel of a gun,” and China’s early communist leaders understood that an army beyond the CCP’s control could threaten the party itself. But this divide has never been as absolute in China as it was in the Soviet system. Early-career officers commonly move between the political and regular command tracks, though such transfers become less frequent once officers reach battalion-level command. As a result, there can be admirals—such as Miao Hua or Yuan Huazhi, both purged last year—who have never commanded a ship. The professional-technical track, meanwhile, encompasses a remarkable variety of jobs, among them rocket engineers, military physicians, military judges, and publishers. In the West, some of these jobs have obvious military equivalents, while others would be held by civilians. (The staffers purged last week from the U.S. military newspaper Stars and Stripes would fall within the Chinese military’s professional-technical ranks.) One example that causes foreign reporters confusion is China’s military academic system. The PLA maintains three prestigious institutions—the Academy of Military Science, the National Defense University, and the National University of Defense Technology—and numerous subordinate schools. The universities are the rough equivalent of the United States’ Naval War College or National Defense University. In the United States, about half of the staff of these institutions are regular officers on temporary teaching assignments, while permanent faculty are usually civilian academics. In China, by contrast, the faculty and staff of military academic institutions were all officers on paper, almost none of which had experience commanding troops, until reforms in 2017 and 2018. They had limited interaction with civilian academia and almost no contact with foreigners, leading to an unusual lack of academic standards. None of this stopped Chinese media from interviewing these scholars and presenting them in uniform. Foreign outlets would commonly report the work of senior professors—called “colonels” or “generals”—as official PLA doctrine. The professors at these institutions were temporarily reclassified as civilian staff in 2018 but appear to have returned to professional-technical status after the 2021 reforms that formalized the division with the officer corps. Professional-technical officers have also been involved with the PLA’s business empire. During the Cultural Revolution, the PLA took over large portions of the Chinese economy, including agricultural and manufacturing enterprises. In 1998, Chinese President Jiang Zemin ordered the PLA’s businesses to be dismantled. However, since they were such wonderful opportunities for personal enrichment, some military-linked businesses still persist, as does the use of PLA-controlled properties by private firms. At least into the early 2010s, it was not unheard of for businesspeople to receive commissioned military rank to run PLA factories or manage military properties. One acquaintance of mine, for instance, ascended from civilian to colonel when he was put in charge of running a condom factory. item.title: What India Gets Out of BRICS
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.64
What India Gets Out of BRICS Ahead of the group’s leaders’ summit, New Delhi is pulling out the stops. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: India gears up for the BRICS leaders’ summit this weekend, Nepal’s youth movement marks its protest anniversary as the country reels from deadly floods, and Bangladesh’s energy crunch puts pressure on the government. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: India gears up for the BRICS leaders’ summit this weekend, Nepal’s youth movement marks its protest anniversary as the country reels from deadly floods, and Bangladesh’s energy crunch puts pressure on the government. New Delhi Preps for BRICS Summit India’s government is pulling out all the stops ahead of the BRICS leaders’ summit hosted in New Delhi on Sept. 12 and 13. Commandos are staging security protocol drills; police are carrying motorcade rehearsals; and city officials are executing a makeover that includes fixing roads, planting flower beds, and deploying BRICS branding. BRICS—named after its original members of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa—has long been a critical institution for India. New Delhi balances its membership in the grouping, meant to provide alternatives to Western economic institutions, with its close ties with the West; in doing so, it bolsters its strategic autonomy. The core goals and priorities of BRICS align with Indian ones: engagement with the global south, advocating for United Nations reform, embracing multilateralism. Most BRICS members are also top Indian partners, and India’s ongoing albeit modest rapprochement with China certainly helps. The grouping expanded in 2024, and aside from Iran, every new member is a close Indian friend. They include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, and the United Arab Emirates. This year’s leaders’ summit, which follows a BRICS foreign ministers’ forum in New Delhi in May, is especially significant for India, though. The high-level summit offers the world’s fastest-growing major economy an opportunity to showcase its convening power and reassert its global leadership. India hasn’t regressed in this realm per se, but in recent months it has been somewhat upstaged in international diplomacy by its rival Pakistan, thanks to Islamabad’s lead mediation role in the Iran war and its increasing influence in the Middle East—from growing arms sales to participation in new bilateral and multilateral defense pacts with regional allies. Further, the BRICS summit provides India with an important space for deeper engagement with the global south amid rising discontent with the Western-led global economic order. New Delhi takes very seriously its goal of becoming a leader of the global south—an objective tied to both its great-power aspirations and historical leadership of the Non-Aligned Movement decades ago. But this effort faces obstacles, especially given India’s limited inroads in Latin America and Africa. Notably, China has a major investment presence in both regions and also seeks to assert itself as a global south leader. The upcoming summit gives Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi a chance to engage bilaterally with the leaders of Brazil and new member Ethiopia. Finally, this weekend’s summit provides India with a platform to make a strong pitch for freer markets and trade and more multilateralism amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s second-term policies, especially high tariffs. These policies probably inspired one of the themes of the summit, economic resilience. This theme is sure to resonate among all BRICS members, and India’s approach aims to ensure consensus for a strong joint statement—an outcome that New Delhi considers essential for a successful summit. The lead-up to BRICS leaders’ summits tends to produce contrasting commentary. One position dismisses the grouping as irrelevant, a talk shop incapable of producing anything of substance. The other celebrates it as a counter to the Western-led global order. Both arguments are flawed: BRICS has produced new initiatives, including its own development bank. At the same time, poor relations among some of the new members, heavy reliance on the U.S. dollar, and a lack of clarity around the group’s ultimate objectives constrain its ability to fully take on the West. Ultimately, BRICS is a significant grouping with considerable limitations. But for India, the calculus is simple: BRICS, warts and all, is a critical vehicle to advance its core foreign-policy interests. What We’re Following Nepal’s youth movement marks anniversary. A year ago this week, young people in Nepal took to the streets to denounce corruption and nepotism. The protests ousted the government in less than 48 hours, ushering in a caretaker government. Elections in March propelled to power the anti-corruption Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), which had never held power before. The RSP-led government helmed by Prime Minister Balendra Shah, the popular 35-year-old former mayor of Kathmandu, didn’t take long to position itself as a very different kind of political player. It released a 100-point governance reform agenda and took unconventional positions; Shah initially refused to meet with foreign officials not of equal or similar rank before changing course. Six months after taking office, the government has been put to the test by the massive floods two weeks ago that killed an estimated 1,400 people in Nepal, with nearly 6,000 still missing. Even amid catastrophe, the government has acted like a maverick, initially declining foreign search-and-rescue teams, and now requesting $20 billion in climate change compensation. Nepal initially called on neighbors China and India to provide aid, but it has asked for support via the U.N. loss and damage fund. Unfortunately for Kathmandu, 119 countries have made similar requests totaling $2.8 billion; only $400 million has been provided. Bangladesh faces pressure on energy crunch. Bangladesh is grappling with a long-running energy crisis, and its new government is feeling pressure to address it. The opposition launched a long march in Dhaka over the weekend, with plans to reach Chittagong. On Monday, opposition leader Shafiqur Rahman, who heads the Jamaat-e-Islami party, said in parliament that Dhaka should establish a task force to tackle the crisis. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party government led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman surely knew that energy would be one of its biggest initial policy challenges when it took office in February. Bangladesh has suffered serious shortages in recent years due to diminishing supplies of domestic fuel. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have worsened the crisis; Bangladesh relies heavily on foreign hydrocarbon imports. Recent industrial accidents, including fires at gas facilities, have made matters worse. Bangladesh has been less successful than many of its South Asian neighbors in embracing renewables to cushion the blow of oil and gas supply shocks. Dhaka recently vowed to expand domestic gas production and tap into clean fuels. But this hasn’t appeased the opposition or a restless public, and Rahman now faces the first major protest movement targeting his government. More violence on Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Last Thursday, Pakistan’s military said it had killed 15 militants attempting to enter the country from Afghanistan. Its statement identified them as members of Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which carries out attacks in Pakistan and which Islamabad accuses the Taliban regime in Afghanistan of sheltering. The links between the TTP and the Taliban—and Pakistan’s contention that Afghanistan provides sanctuary to the militants—have sparked serious tensions between the two countries since the Taliban returned to power in 2021. The Taliban have not responded publicly to the Pakistani military’s recent statement. This silence is striking, given that the Taliban have repeatedly rejected claims that they shelter militants. The lack of response might indicate ongoing third-party efforts to ease tensions: Last week, the Chinese and Pakistani special envoys for Afghanistan reportedly met in Islamabad. However, previous external mediation efforts have failed to end the crisis. Islamabad continues to insist that the Taliban regime provide verifiable and written assurances that bases on Afghan soil won’t be used for terrorism against Pakistan. Under the Radar Last Wednesday, Sri Lanka announced that U.S. and Sri Lankan officials had busted a large drug smuggling operation that was attempting to use the country as a stop on the way to international markets. Sri Lankan police said anti-narcotics authorities from both countries seized about half a ton of crystal methamphetamine that arrived in a shipping container the previous weekend. Two Pakistani citizens were reportedly arrested in the sting. The U.S. Embassy in Colombo made a similar announcement, noting that $2 million worth of drugs were found hidden in bath towels in the shipping container. But this story has a curious twist. On Friday, Pakistan’s anti-narcotics agency issued its own statement announcing that Islamabad had worked with partners in the United States and Sri Lanka to bust a narcotics trafficking network. Pakistani officials said the raid in Sri Lanka was preceded by a Pakistani operation in Karachi in July. Additionally, while the U.S. and Sri Lankan statements described the drug ring as Pakistan-based, the Pakistani statement said it originated in Afghanistan. The reason for this discrepancy is unclear, though Pakistan would have an incentive to downplay drug trafficking on its own soil and emphasize the culpability of Afghanistan. Either way, trilateral cooperation between the United States and partners in South Asia is unusual. But in this case, it would make sense: Washington currently has warm ties with both Colombo and Islamabad, and Sri Lanka is one of Pakistan’s few close friends in the region. FP’s Most Read This Week - Trump’s Venezuela Oil Deal Is a Farce by Keith Johnson - Trump Has Peaked by Ravi Agrawal - Welcome to the New Defense-Dominant World by Stephen M. Walt Regional Voices In the Indian Express, journalist Aakash Joshi laments the killing of Chongtham Vikram Singh, a musician and member of an ethnic minority from India’s Manipur state. “Between the many whys and the single how of a murder in Delhi, there’s all the anger, inequality, bigotry and dehumanization that we accept every day,” he writes. A scathing Kathmandu Post editorial accuses Nepal’s government of reneging on its reform pledges a year after the Gen Z protests: “The most profound failure of accountability is the treatment of those who bled for this political change. A year later, wounded protesters are trapped in state neglect while new leaders thrive.” In the Daily Star, scholar Manzoor Ahmed argues that Bangladesh must adapt new strategies for combating illiteracy, which remains a persistent challenge. “Technology could help reshape how foundational skills are taught, moving away from rigid, under-resourced classrooms towards flexible learning environments,” he writes Michael Kugelman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly South Asia Brief and a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council. An analyst of the region for nearly two decades, he previously directed the South Asia Institute at the Wilson Center. item.title: Are Yemen and Saudi Arabia Returning to All-Out War?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.63
Are Yemen and Saudi Arabia Returning to All-Out War? Houthi strikes risk adding a new front to the Iran conflict. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure, Canada’s latest retaliatory tariffs against the United States, and a British ban on all Israeli goods made in the West Bank. ‘Dangerous Escalation’ Houthi rebels in Yemen launched a slew of missile and drone attacks across Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, marking one of the largest Houthi assaults on the kingdom since fighting erupted in July. The strikes mark another major escalation between Riyadh and the Iranian proxy group, and they raise fears that renewed fighting could transform into all-out war. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure, Canada’s latest retaliatory tariffs against the United States, and a British ban on all Israeli goods made in the West Bank. ‘Dangerous Escalation’ Houthi rebels in Yemen launched a slew of missile and drone attacks across Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, marking one of the largest Houthi assaults on the kingdom since fighting erupted in July. The strikes mark another major escalation between Riyadh and the Iranian proxy group, and they raise fears that renewed fighting could transform into all-out war. Early Tuesday, the Houthi rebel group accused Saudi Arabia of targeting a Yemeni prison in Jawf province, killing at least 17 people and wounding around seven others. “Every aggression against our country and people will be met with a firm response,” Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesperson, warned on Tuesday. Hours later, Saudi military officials said that the Houthis had targeted four Saudi cities, injuring more than 70 people, including women and children. According to Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, the strikes also damaged critical civilian and military infrastructure, including oil facilities connected to Bab el-Mandeb strait, a logistics hub on the Red Sea coast, and King Khalid Air Base, located near Khamis Mushait. These strikes signal a “dangerous escalation,” and the Saudi-led coalition will take “all necessary measures and actions to respond to the sources of the threat,” Maliki said on Tuesday. In September 2014, Houthi forces seized control of Yemen’s capital, sparking a devastating civil war. In 2015, a coalition of countries led by Saudi Arabia intervened militarily to try to restore power to Yemen’s internationally recognized government. Although a 2022 truce largely eased fighting between the two forces, the Iran war’s destabilization of the region has risked upending that delicate detente, particularly after the Saudi-led military coalition attacked Sanaa International Airport in July to prevent a plane carrying Houthis flying back from Tehran from landing. Since then, the Houthis have tried to advance on government-held positions, while Yemeni authorities have said that they aim to recapture all Houthi-held territory. According to the World Health Organization, renewed conflict killed at least 194 people and injured more than 880 others between Aug. 23 and Sept. 5. That includes at least 81 people killed during a Houthi ground assault near Bab el-Mandeb, which was part of a wider rebel effort to control traffic through the critical waterway; Bab el-Mandeb connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a vital alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. Global energy prices reeled on Tuesday in the wake of the Houthis’ missile and drone attack. Brent crude briefly surpassed $99 per barrel for the first time since late July, and West Texas Intermediate hit its highest level since early June. Today’s Most Read - What Was the War on Terror? by Joseph Stieb - 25 Years After 9/11, What Are We Failing to Imagine Now? by Colin P. Clarke and Clara Broekaert - The Conservative Case for International Law by Luke Nicastro and Heather Penatzer What We’re Following “Dollar for dollar.” Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on around $20 billion worth of U.S. goods went into effect on Tuesday. The duties, which impact goods from textiles to cheese to furniture, mimic recent tariffs that the White House has imposed on Ottawa, and they signal the latest bout of escalatory measures in the two economies’ expanding trade war. Last month, trade negotiations between U.S. and Canadian officials collapsed after Ottawa accused Washington of trying to destroy key Canadian industries. Both U.S. President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a slew of tariffs in response, with Ottawa pledging to go “dollar for dollar” with the White House’s duties. Accompanied by a war of words between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford, relations between the North American neighbors have reached one of their lowest points in years. Canada’s latest tariffs—and its larger pivot away from the United States as its No. 1 trading partner—“will come at a cost,” Carney said in a video message on Tuesday. However, “it doesn’t come close to the cost of standing still,” he added. Just hours before Tuesday’s duties took effect, Trump took aim at Canadian plane manufacturer Bombardier on Truth Social, suggesting that the company will no longer be allowed to sell its products in the United States. “BUY AMERICAN. FLY ON AMERICAN AIRLINERS. ENJOY AMERICAN LIQUOR AND BEVERAGES. SAIL ON LAKE AMERICA,” Trump wrote. Last month, he signed an executive order requiring Lake Ontario to be renamed as “Lake America” in the U.S. federal government’s geographic names information system. Punishing Israel. The United Kingdom announced its intention on Tuesday to impose sweeping trade restrictions on Israel, including a ban on all goods produced in the occupied West Bank. “Today marks the beginning of a new approach,” British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament, calling Israeli settlements in the West Bank “unlawful” and accusing extremist settlers of perpetrating “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians.” He added, “To those who finance or facilitate illegal settlements, let me say this: You will face the full force of U.K. sanctions.” Miliband’s announcement cements London’s support for an International Court of Justice ruling in July 2024 that found Israel’s presence in the West Bank to be in violation of international law, including prohibitions on racial segregation and apartheid. It also lends support to similar trade bans by Canada and France, which have denounced Israel’s occupation of the West Bank. Although Western criticism of Israel’s West Bank occupation has grown in recent years, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has continued to shrug off foreign condemnation, and several of his cabinet members have repeatedly pushed for the construction of more settlements. On Tuesday, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar announced that Israel will close the British consulate in Jerusalem, expel British representatives monitoring the Gaza cease-fire, end U.K. training of Palestinian Authority security forces in the West Bank, and bar 12 elected British officials from entering Israel, among other retaliatory measures. An AfD victory. Thousands of people held a pro-democracy rally in Berlin on Tuesday to denounce the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party’s recent state election win. Carrying signs condemning some of the AfD’s trademark policies—including its anti-immigrant and pro-Russian stances—the backlash foreshadows what experts suspect will be two more tumultuous regional elections later this month. On Sunday, the AfD won a landslide victory in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt. With around 44 percent of the vote, this was a nativist party’s best-ever state election showing since the Nazi regime. Germany’s mainstream parties have long vowed to never work with the AfD, and the far-right party is classified as an extremist group in some regions of the country, including in Saxony-Anhalt. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has already ruled out any collaboration with the AfD, doubling down on the country’s so-called firewall against the far-right group. However, the hard-left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance has signaled its intention to form a governing alliance with the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt. Odds and Ends First, the Louvre. Then, Paris’s Museum of Natural History. On Tuesday, another French collection joined the list of museums targeted by art heists in recent months. Investigators said a group of “well-equipped” and “well-informed” thieves sliced through a fence to enter the Renoir Museum in the French Riviera’s Cagnes-sur-Mer, stealing four valuable paintings. Local police arrived around five minutes after the alarm was triggered, forcing the suspects to abandon two of the masterpieces in the museum’s garden. However, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Young Woman at the Well are still missing, and the culprits remain at large.
