item.title: How to Survive in a World Without Rules
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.35
Not so long ago, it seemed that the world was becoming more civilized. The end of the Cold War was supposed to bring the triumph of the rules-based order. Enlightened norms and cooperation, buttressed by a broad-minded superpower, would supplant anarchic patterns of the past. It was an inspiring vision—and, alas, an illusion. Now, all around the world, rules are in retreat. Aggression and conquest are surging; economic coercion and predation are rampant. Respect for international law and organizations is cratering; arms control is in decline. Great powers are reviving dreams of empire; the United States is tempted to seek narrow national aggrandizement at the cost of world order. And as global norms falter, strong leaders are shredding political constraints and institutions at home. Not so long ago, it seemed that the world was becoming more civilized. The end of the Cold War was supposed to bring the triumph of the rules-based order. Enlightened norms and cooperation, buttressed by a broad-minded superpower, would supplant anarchic patterns of the past. It was an inspiring vision—and, alas, an illusion. Now, all around the world, rules are in retreat. Aggression and conquest are surging; economic coercion and predation are rampant. Respect for international law and organizations is cratering; arms control is in decline. Great powers are reviving dreams of empire; the United States is tempted to seek narrow national aggrandizement at the cost of world order. And as global norms falter, strong leaders are shredding political constraints and institutions at home. Our world is at risk of becoming a gangster’s paradise, in which rules matter far less than they once did—and raw power matters more. This is a harsh shift for those whose mindsets were made in a kinder moment. It will present severe tests for leaders who must navigate an unforgiving age. There’s little utility, at this point, in lamenting the fall of the post-Cold War order. The task is to understand the requirements of survival in our post-rules world. The purpose of this essay, therefore, is to sketch a map of the new era we’re entering and provide some guidelines for making the best of the bad times ahead. The dream of a rules-based order is fading into history, but there was a time when it seemed like the future. After World War II, Washington and its Western allies built half a rules-based order—a set of deeply cooperative relationships, structured by shared norms and supranational institutions—within the free world as a way of containing the Kremlin. Once the Soviet bloc collapsed and the Cold War ended, there was a chance to take that project global. The core of the rules-based order was the idea that old, destructive impulses could be overcome through the adoption of liberal practices and principles—and the consistent application of U.S. power. A flourishing, open economy would enrich all participants; commercial disputes would be resolved through World Trade Organization (WTO) procedures, not mutually immiserating tariff fights. Habits of conquest and domination would be discouraged; vital norms, such as freedom of navigation and respect for borders, would be strengthened. Freed from Cold War paralysis, international organizations and law would gain influence. Great-power rivalry itself would fade as potential spoilers—a rising China, a resurgent Russia—became satisfied stakeholders in a system that delivered prosperity and peace. That vision was an effort to tame the destructive forces that had repeatedly torn the world apart in the 20th century. It wasn’t as utopian as it might seem in hindsight: Just as laws are enforced by sheriffs, the rules-based order rested upon U.S. power. The U.S. Navy beat back piracy and other threats to freedom of the seas; the Pentagon anchored alliances that deterred aggression; Washington rallied coalitions that fought terrorism, rogue-state proliferation, and other scourges. The rules-based order was made in America: Washington, more than any other actor, set the terms of international stability. The country’s preferred concepts—free markets, democracy, human rights—advanced around the globe. Russian President Vladimir Putin wasn’t wholly wrong when he angrily alleged, in 2007, that the rules-based order was a cloak for U.S. hegemony. That’s part, but only part, of why that order came undone. Rules are never value-free, and Washington’s rules seemed oppressive, even existentially threatening, to autocratic regimes that sought to crush liberal impulses at home while building empires abroad. Putin’s Russia began forcibly changing borders in the post-Soviet space as soon as it regained the strength to do so. China plunged into the global economy and used the explosive growth that followed to fund a record-busting military buildup, a determined campaign to dominate the industries of the future, and a bid to dominate the South China Sea. Washington’s rules prevailed in a unipolar environment. They sagged as the balance shifted—and America soured on its own global project. The United States had always taken a selective approach to rule-following: It waged wars, in Kosovo and Iraq, without the blessing of the United Nations. But then something more fundamental changed. Americans became tired of playing sheriff after draining Middle East fights and a global financial crisis: By 2013-14, U.S. President Barack Obama was declining to enforce his own red line against Syrian strongman Bashar al-Assad’s chemical weapons attacks against his population and doing little to contest Russia’s first invasion of Ukraine. Frustration followed fatigue: Persistent allied free-riding led politicians from both major parties to argue that the United States was bearing too much responsibility for global order and reaping too few benefits. Perhaps most damaging, China’s meteoric rise produced a sense that the system worked against U.S. interests—that an open world economy had eviscerated U.S. manufacturing and enriched a ruthless rival. The rules-based order came to seem like a burden, or perhaps a bad deal, for its chief defender. Now, we’re in a new moment, as that order comes undone. We’re a long way from a rules-based economy: Commercial and strategic rivalries are ripping that system apart. The WTO has been moribund for years as countries take trade fights into their own hands. Protectionism proliferates as governments try to dominate key industries or defend them from foreign competition: Tariffs and other trade-distorting measures were rising before U.S. President Donald Trump’s onslaught in 2025. The United States and China are wielding their control of key supply chains against each other as tools of economic coercion and geopolitical competition. The global economy has become a battleground as countries clash for power and cast aside once respected rules. Developing countries that profited enormously from trade and investment flows under the old system—even as they resented, often bitterly, its inequities—face tougher growth prospects in a world with higher walls. Likewise, the global security environment grows more disordered. The post-Cold War peace is over: Levels of state-based conflict have reached their highest mark in decades. Arms control frameworks—whether U.S.-Russia nuclear agreements or international accords against the use of land mines—are crumbling. Territorial expansion is becoming commonplace as countries from China to Rwanda encroach upon neighbors; Russia’s effort to eradicate Ukraine is only the most egregious example of that disturbing trend. And as interstate violence rises, respect for international law and organizations plummets. The notion that the U.N. Security Council is the arbiter of anything seems quaint. Respect for borders isn’t the only norm in trouble. Gone are the days when leaders touted a “responsibility to protect” peoples victimized by their own rulers. Impunity prevails as atrocities against civilians increase and powerful autocracies pay scant price for their crimes. China, for example, has engaged in industrial-scale repression against Uyghurs and suffered only modest scrutiny from international organizations and trade partners. Transnational repression is on the upswing as dictators hound their critics around the world. Meanwhile, the norm that underpins global trade—freedom of navigation—is under violent assault. China’s offensive in the South China Sea, the Houthi campaign against Red Sea shipping, Russia’s claims to sovereignty over the Northern Sea Route, and Iran’s Strait of Hormuz chokehold are all indicative of a trend in which predatory actors try to enclose the seas. This isn’t full-blown anarchy; the rules-based order may be yielding to a neoimperial age. For years, U.S. policymakers argued that spheres of influence were an impermissible anachronism. Yet China is building a traditional sphere of influence on its territorial and maritime peripheries, a vast arc spanning from the Himalayas to the East China Sea; it is also building a digital sphere encompassing huge swaths of the global south. Russia uses strategic corruption and brutal aggression to assert its writ in parts of Central Asia and Eastern Europe. Turkey and Israel have effectively carved up a post-Assad Syria; Ankara seeks an Ottoman revival in North Africa and the Middle East. Then there’s Washington’s imperial restoration: The United States has turned Venezuela into a vassal state and claimed an entire hemisphere as its domain. It exacts tribute from allies around the Eurasian periphery. Institution-breaking at home enables norm-busting abroad. Two decades ago, a U.S. president could tout the coming triumph of democratic institutions. Now, a panoply of democratic, semi-democratic, and autocratic leaders—Trump, Putin, China’s Xi Jinping, India’s Narendra Modi, and Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdogan—are demolishing constraints on their authority. They are building personalized polities around the strength and charisma of a dynamic leader. Xi’s deconstruction of term limits has allowed him to pursue a generational strategy of Chinese restoration. Trump’s disdain for checks and balances enables tariff wars, dodgy economic deals, and surprising resorts to force. Domestic and international politics evolve in parallel—and the United States is playing a catalytic role in this post-rules world. To be fair, Trump’s record isn’t pure rule-breaking. On his watch, the U.S. military has brawled with bad actors—the Houthis and Iran—that are waging war against freedom of navigation. Trump struck a blow for nonproliferation by smashing Iran’s nuclear facilities in June 2025. His administration has sought to broker peace in locales from sub-Saharan Africa to Southeast Asia; it has exerted sharp pressure against roguish governments in Caracas, Havana, and Tehran. It has continued, albeit ambivalently, to support Ukraine against Russia. And if the president isn’t a stickler for moral niceties, he and his advisors argue that ruthlessness is the price of survival in a cutthroat world. A superpower that fetishizes global rules, in this telling, disarms itself against foes that flout them. Washington can’t play by WTO standards if China doesn’t; it can’t let international law shield governments that consort with drug traffickers, sponsor terrorism, or seek the world’s worst weapons. There’s something to these arguments: Global order does require that the United States be resolute in defending its interests. The problem is that Trump has also made common cause, implicitly or explicitly, with revisionist actors tearing the old system down. Trump periodically tries to turn global public goods into protection rackets—for example, by declaring that Washington will control and toll shipping through Hormuz. His administration lacerated the global trade system with tariffs and has ignored international law in carrying out lethal strikes against alleged drug traffickers in the Western Hemisphere. Impunity appeals to Trump: He reportedly proposed that Beijing, Moscow, and Washington cooperate to paralyze the International Criminal Court. And Trump has joined the revisionists in a more fundamental sense—by using economic pressure and threats of violence in bids to extort territorial concessions from weaker states. Many U.S. allies fear that Trump will break any rule that constrains his ambition—perhaps because that’s exactly what the president sometimes says. After ordering the January snatch of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Trump declared that only his own morality—not international law or the U.S. Constitution—could constrain him. “We live in a world … that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power,” White House official Stephen Miller added. “These are the iron laws of the world that have existed since the beginning of time.” Fortunately, the world is nowhere near the levels of violence and anarchy of the 1930s or other blighted eras. Many alliances and institutions that have long fostered stability are being challenged—but remain intact. What’s clear is that the world is becoming darker, more disordered, and less forgiving of leaders who neglect the realities of this dawning age. What, then, are the requirements of survival in a post-rules world? The first imperative is to recognize that nostalgia isn’t a strategy. It’s tempting for U.S. allies and others who relied on the rules-based order to make Trump the sole villain of this story, to hope that U.S. policy—and global conditions—will snap back once he leaves the scene. It’s probably true that the next U.S. president won’t be hell-bent on grabbing Greenland. Yet Trump isn’t the only source of trouble: Beijing and Moscow were assailing the rules-based order long before he was ever elected president. Trump is a symptom of deeper changes—the insecurities of interdependence, the resurgence of great-power rivalry—that will outlast his time in office. Leaders do matter, and there are critical uncertainties about the future of U.S. policy. But whoever becomes president in 2028 or 2032, don’t expect that the world will revert to a fundamentally gentler state. Countries that root their mindsets in this new era will be better able to handle its vicissitudes. Those that defer hard decisions are headed for trouble. Indeed, if America’s European allies often seem so off-balance, perhaps that’s because the continent’s most ingrained habits—its optimism that the bad old ways could be banished, its continual invocation of the rules-based order, its chronic underinvestment in the tools of self-protection—are products of a prior age. Even as European rearmament accelerates, legacy commitments linger: Most countries won’t reach ambitious military spending targets unless they pare back domestic entitlement programs that swelled during decades when Washington covered so much of the tab for NATO’s defense. That’s a tough trade-off but one the new era will require. Thus, a second rule: Self-help is vital in a vicious world. There are fewer protections against predation at the hands of revisionists; there’s decreased certainty that a benevolent great power will counteract the malevolent ones. Countries that rely solely on their alliance with Washington are risking disappointment with fatal implications; those that bank on international law, multilateral institutions, or moral principle risk becoming prey for stronger foes. Self-help gets a bad name in the academic literature, where it is associated with lawless, dog-eat-dog behavior. Yet in present conditions, self-help is eminently rational: It’s a matter of developing the sovereign capabilities and alternative coalitions that can extend an exposed state’s life. Poland and Japan are models: They are making historic defense investments that blow through old fiscal and political barriers. They are cultivating new coalitions as complements to their existing alliances—whether the nascent Intermarium concept, in which Warsaw cooperates more closely with other front-line states in Europe, or the quasi-alliances Japan has built with Australia and the Philippines and the deepening defense relationships it has cultivated with states from India to Vietnam. This path—preserving as much cooperation as possible with Washington while simultaneously creating stronger hedges against an uncertain future—is the best one available to allies that can’t fully depend on U.S. power but can’t do without it, either. It also buys time to consider whether more radical forms of self-help, such as acquiring nuclear weapons, might one day be necessary. This self-help surge illustrates a third principle: Don’t bet on cooperation among middle powers to save the old system, even if such cooperation can mitigate the damage caused by the system’s demise. In January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made himself a Davos darling by touting a middle-power moment, in which supporters of the rules-based order would come together to sustain it against Beijing and Washington alike. But that’s a big ask. If middle powers could set the terms of global order, they wouldn’t be middle powers. Power realities are stubborn: There’s no plausible middle-power coalition that can contain China without support from the United States. The Carney concept also exaggerates middle-power unity. Some key players, such as Brazil, India, and Saudi Arabia, see as much opportunity as danger in a fragmented environment; they are ambivalent at best about an order that was built by the West. Efforts to forge a grand middle-power coalition will likely prove a waste of time and energy. The smarter approach is for smaller, more cohesive groups to find ways of limiting their vulnerability and dependence in a world with fewer guarantees. It’s eminently reasonable for Europe to gradually reduce its reliance on the U.S. market through deals with India and Mercosur—just as it is reasonable for India, Mercosur, and other developing economies to broaden their commercial options as U.S. tariff barriers rise. It’s prudent for Japan to foster Asian defense supply chains that might one day shore up the front line against China while mitigating technological dependence on Washington. It makes sense for Canada to cooperate more closely on Arctic security with the Scandinavian countries as great-power pressure mounts from several different directions. In a self-help world, resilience at the margin is worth seeking—even if there’s no good near-term substitute to working with the United States. Fourth, even as U.S. alliances become less special, Washington and its friends must still find ways of ensuring that those alliances endure. Whatever Trump says, the United States still needs alliances in Europe, the Middle East, and Asia: It can’t act as a global heavyweight without the strategic real estate and military access they provide. Likewise, Washington may have the best artificial intelligence models, but it can’t dominate the AI age without the help of friends, from the Netherlands to Taiwan, that occupy key nodes in the global tech stack. Even a self-interested superpower still needs help. And whatever their concerns about Washington, U.S. allies still need those pacts for protection against nearby gangsters, whether China, Iran, North Korea, or Russia. Even if those allies can balance against their adversaries without U.S. backing in the future, they must avoid the piercing vulnerability that a break with Washington would bring between now and then. Sure, self-help becomes more important as U.S. power becomes less reliable. But for the time being, front-line countries from South Korea to Finland prefer imperfect, uncertain alliances with the United States to the costs and risks of going it alone. Even allies that need U.S. support won’t want to rely on it too heavily, of course. Events in recent years have made it tougher to argue the idea that U.S. security pacts are rooted in shared values. By making U.S. defense commitments more conditional, Trump has made the specter of abandonment all too real. So the task for Washington and its allies will be to find a more transactional basis for their economic, military, and technological collaboration—for example, pacts that trade allied support in securing and strengthening AI supply chains for privileged access to U.S. computing power and frontier models. The key is to preserve the ability to work together on common interests even as institutions that once anchored the free world become wary partnerships rather than enduring communities of strategic trust. Fifth, if the dilemmas of the new era are sharpest for U.S. allies, countries everywhere should prepare to pay rising risk premiums in a disordered environment. Realists roll their eyes at talk of “global norms.” Yet some of those norms, namely freedom of navigation, constitute the foundation of world trade. Virtually all countries, from developing nations to onetime colonial powers, have profited massively from the stability and openness of the global commons. An era in which those norms crumble is one in which shipping and insurance costs shoot upward, supply chains are violently disrupted, and economic friction multiplies. And as the recent Persian Gulf war has demonstrated, the United States may not have the ability to uphold freedom of navigation in contested waters, even when it summons the will. This makes workarounds—even cost-intensive ones—for maritime chokepoints crucial. An expanded pipeline network that brings Gulf oil to the world, while bypassing Hormuz, is an expensive but essential insurance policy—and a way of gradually decreasing the leverage Iran can exert. Likewise, the weaponization of energy flows, critical minerals stocks, and other aspects of interdependence necessitates a broader shift from efficiency to resilience. As blockades, embargoes, and other sanctions become the warp and woof of the world economy, prudent actors should be willing to pay a premium for insulation from coercive threats. This applies, unfortunately, to poorer states as well: As conflict roils food and energy distribution networks, even developing countries may need to invest in the creation of larger strategic reserves. This all sounds so promising for the world’s revisionist states. The collapse of the rules-based order opens the way to the pursuit of their designs. But a sixth imperative is that those states should be careful what they wish for: A gangster’s world might not suit them forever, even if it energizes them for a while. Xi and Putin will surely profit as Washington weakens international law and flirts with violent expansion. They’ll delight when U.S. alliances—the principal hard-power barriers to their own aggrandizement—come under doubt. In a world without rules, the returns to ruthless behavior increase. Take a longer view, however, and those dividends could dwindle over time. If countries concerned about aggressive autocracies and an erratic America end up arming themselves feverishly, that won’t necessarily end well for Putin, Xi, and their ilk. We’ll see how much China likes facing a Japan bristling with weapons as it casts off historical shackles on its foreign policy or whether Russia’s strategic situation improves once Polish and German military muscles are bulging and those countries are no longer constrained by the United States. If rampant insecurity eventually brings rampant nuclear proliferation, both Beijing and Moscow could face tenser, more dangerous conditions in their home regions. In a truly zero-sum era, everyone could end up less secure. Moreover, China’s trade-dependent economy still needs safe seas and foreign markets. If the international economy fragments and freedom of navigation falters, Beijing may miss the rules-based order after all. Finally, leaders must consider a seventh reality: Different futures are still possible—and much depends on whether the United States can summon a targeted, enlightened ruthlessness or not. In one, more desirable scenario, Washington recognizes that it can’t restrain remorseless rivals while worshipping rules; it adopts a gangster’s ethos in combating autocratic powers that trample borders and try to dominate the world economy. But it accepts, as it did during the Cold War, that there’s one set of standards in dealing with friends and another in dealing with enemies; U.S. officials understand the need to go easier on allies so they can, collectively, push back harder against China and other foes. If this scenario materializes after Trump leaves office, then a turbulent era need not be disastrous. A vital, transactional baseline of allied cooperation could endure on issues from securing rare-earth and semiconductor supply chains to shoring up the Western Pacific military balance. In fact, a brush with abandonment during the Trump era might convince allies that it’s in their interest to offer more of the help Washington needs if the democratic community is to out-compete its foes. If, however, the United States keeps pursuing coercion in all directions, the world—and eventually Washington—will end up in a harsher place. A true gangster’s paradise might, initially, benefit the United States. Raw power counts for more when standards of behavior are debased. What country would fare better in a might-makes-right environment than a superpower with more might than anyone else? That’s the short-term allure of a zero-sum agenda. The long game looks less inviting. U.S. support for a broadly beneficial order has lubricated its power by giving it greater global legitimacy. Alliance relationships have been eased by the sense that the United States is basically a decent country, even if it sometimes does distasteful things. If Washington adopts a gangster’s ethos, it will rupture the relationships that have magnified its influence. It will give other countries greater incentive to withhold their cooperation or even find ways of pushing back. Principle is a fount of power. If Washington forgets that, it will pay a heavy price. The post-Cold War era was a time when the light of progress shone so brightly. Our unfolding era promises to be darker and, perhaps, more desperate. It’s all the more critical, then, for leaders to mentally map the contours of this moment—if only so they can better navigate the dangers it presents. Hal Brands is the Henry A. Kissinger distinguished professor of global affairs at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, and managing director at Macro Advisory Partners. item.title: How to Write Better Rules for Global Finance
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.19
A world without rules is a frightening prospect. But before we mourn the passing of the old order, we should be honest about what its rules were designed to do. The architecture that has governed the global economy for the past 80 years was never a neutral system serving everyone equally. The Bretton Woods system, created in 1944, established institutions such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank to protect and promote peace, stability, and development, yet it encoded the interests of a small group of wealthy nations from the start. What is fraying today, amid resurgent nationalism and geopolitical tensions of a kind not seen since World War II, is not the rule of law in the global economy; it is the legitimacy of rules that socialized risks while privatizing rewards and that gave a majority of the world’s countries—and people—little voice in the decisions that shaped their futures. The task ahead is therefore not to restore the old order, or to resign ourselves to a lawless vacuum, but to write new rules around a different organizing principle: the common good. A world without rules is a frightening prospect. But before we mourn the passing of the old order, we should be honest about what its rules were designed to do. The architecture that has governed the global economy for the past 80 years was never a neutral system serving everyone equally. The Bretton Woods system, created in 1944, established institutions such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank to protect and promote peace, stability, and development, yet it encoded the interests of a small group of wealthy nations from the start. What is fraying today, amid resurgent nationalism and geopolitical tensions of a kind not seen since World War II, is not the rule of law in the global economy; it is the legitimacy of rules that socialized risks while privatizing rewards and that gave a majority of the world’s countries—and people—little voice in the decisions that shaped their futures. The task ahead is therefore not to restore the old order, or to resign ourselves to a lawless vacuum, but to write new rules around a different organizing principle: the common good. Currently, economic policy is trapped in a harmful cycle. The global system treats markets as natural and efficient, while it casts governments as fixers of “market failures,” intervening only when things go wrong—a public good here, a subsidy there, a bailout when crisis hits. But a framework built on failures is, by definition, negative and reactive. So long as “public goods” are understood merely as what the private sector fails to provide, we do not have a theory of the public good; we have a theory of what the private sector is missing. The same logic plays out internationally: As long as the global system treats challenges such as pandemic preparedness, water security, and a stable climate as gaps that it must fill through aid, charity, and after-the-fact corrections, we will keep picking up the pieces of crises we could have prevented. The common good is not what is left over once failures are corrected. It is an objective we must choose and reach together. Reaching it requires paying attention to how economic actors, including governments, businesses, workers, and communities, relate to one another. Just as an orchestra is judged not only on what it plays but on how its musicians play together, economies must be evaluated not only on what they produce but on how participants collaborate with and value one another. Markets are always shaped—by rules, incentives, and institutions. The question is not whether to shape them but whether we direct them toward collective flourishing or let them drift wherever the loudest soloist, or the strongest actor, dictates. To hold that direction—and to ensure that the “common good” does not become another meaningless slogan—the international community needs a framework to guide its reforms and decision-making. A common-good compass should consist of five elements: purpose and directionality, co-creation and participation, collective learning and knowledge sharing, access for all and reward sharing, and transparency and accountability. It is the interaction of all five that matters. Neglect any one, and the framework will be captured by special interests. Nowhere is this compass more urgently needed than in the institutions that govern global finance. The IMF and World Bank carry the words “international” and “world” in their names, but their decision-making power remains concentrated in a handful of countries in the global north, while the global south, which is home to a majority of the world’s population and the principal recipient of their programs, has minimal say. In order to construct an international order worthy of the name, the world must begin by redesigning these institutions. It is important to recognize that there has been a shift in recent years by new IMF and World Bank leadership toward greater decentralization within these institutions, with efforts to strengthen country-level leadership, operational capacity, and responsiveness to local contexts. While still limited in scope, these steps reflect growing recognition that legitimacy and effectiveness depend increasingly on proximity to the realities and priorities of borrowing countries rather than on decisions concentrated in Washington or other headquarters. Nonetheless, inequitable governance structures continue to prevent deep and transformative reforms from taking place. In both the IMF and World Bank, voting power is based on financial contributions, not democratic representation. This gives disproportionate influence to wealthy nations, especially the United States, which maintains de facto veto power in the IMF. Meanwhile, most countries in the global south frequently pay higher borrowing costs and must comply with conditions that can undermine domestic policy and development goals. The consequences have been severe. Between 1970 and 2023, global south countries paid a staggering $2.2 trillion in interest to Western creditors. Heavy debt burdens have drained resources from essential public services, while austerity-driven structural adjustment programs have curtailed government spending, restricted taxation of transnational corporations, and hindered domestic industrial development. As a result, the global south has become increasingly dependent on foreign borrowing. Today, more than 3 billion people—including roughly 57 percent of Africa’s total population—live in countries that spend more on debt servicing than on education or healthcare. Many problems in the global south are rooted in the historical development of the global north, which must take responsibility for providing solutions. This includes financing climate mitigation and development through grants and official development assistance, rather than relying primarily on loans. Philanthropy, while often well intentioned, is also not sufficient, as it obscures the deeper structural issues it claims to address. For instance, the Bezos Earth Fund, established by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, has made important investments in climate adaptation. Yet it is funded by wealth generated through deeply problematic business practices. Amazon has relied on tax avoidance and labor exploitation to accumulate massive profits while also producing 80.9 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2025, comparable to a midsize European country. Its carbon footprint is expected to grow further due to its data center expansion. While the Bezos Earth Fund provides some support for addressing climate change, it cannot offset the harm caused by Amazon’s core business practices. Similarly, the Gates Foundation has played a significant role in global health, contributing more than $100 billion since 1994 and supporting lifesaving vaccines for diseases such as malaria. Yet while vaccines can reduce child deaths, a broader public health approach that ensures universal access to clean water and sanitation would address the root causes of these diseases. It is true that governments are responsible for building these systems, but corporate tax avoidance and the use of restrictive intellectual property rights by companies including Microsoft—the source of the Gates Foundation’s wealth—have exacerbated gaps in public health infrastructure. Real development requires investment in local and national capacity, including building a capable civil service and diversifying economies beyond natural resources into sectors such as digital services and manufacturing. In other words, development demands that actors in the global north, including philanthropic ones, engage in well-designed partnerships that reflect the principles of the common good and support a degree of autonomy, enabling global south countries to lead their own development agendas. Unfortunately, many of the solutions that international institutions have proposed to address development challenges in the global south have been ineffective efforts to patch over problems rooted in a deeply inequitable financial system, without reforming the system itself. One such approach is “blended finance,” the strategic use of public funding to attract private investment. This gained recognition in the 2010s as a tool to mobilize additional resources to address the lack of progress on the Sustainable Development Goals, or SDGs, which all United Nations members adopted in 2015 as a global framework for assessing national well-being. The logic was that public resources could “crowd in” private capital, turning “billions into trillions.” Yet the lack of progress over the past decade suggests that the problem lies not only in the scale of finance but in the system’s design and incentives. At its peak, blended finance mobilized only around $15 billion per year—less than 0.4 percent of SDG financing needs. Moreover, the majority of these funds originated from public or concessional sources rather than new private investment, while the projects that did attract private participation were often in already profitable sectors or middle-income countries. These outcomes highlight the need for a deeper structural transformation in development finance. The World Bank and other development banks have recently begun to move away from the “billions to trillions” narrative toward a catalytic approach, using innovative financial instruments and updated policies to mobilize investment and expand their lending capacity without compromising financial integrity. For instance, the World Bank is experimenting with risk-sharing tools, such as the International Finance Corp.’s first collateralized loan obligation. It has also introduced new mechanisms, such as hybrid capital and the Livable Planet Fund, to support climate resilience, food security, and pandemic preparedness. These efforts reflect a move toward “more, but better, debt,” accompanied by transparent reporting and mutually agreed conditions that protect fiscal sustainability. While this progress is encouraging, the challenge ahead is to ensure that these reforms contribute to a deeper transformation of the international financial architecture. This is a matter not only of finance but also of governance and power. Genuine reform requires a shift to a system that grants all countries true ownership of global priorities. The common-good compass offers a practical guide for reforming the international financial system in ways that truly serve people and communities. Consider again the five elements of the compass. First, direction matters because investments and finance must create real, measurable impact, rather than simply circulating through global markets or de-risking private activity. All stakeholders, including countries in the global south, must shape that direction. Institutions thus need new governance structures that bring all countries to the table, instead of perpetuating a system where the richest nations make decisions that often come at the expense of poorer ones. Tackling global challenges such as pandemics and climate change also demands structured collaboration and knowledge sharing—for example, through patent pools, which are agreements between organizations or states to license patents collectively. Such mechanisms have proved especially valuable during health crises and could help develop solutions to pressing issues such as clean energy and technology access. Equally important is the fair distribution of the rewards from collective investments. The benefits derived from the extraction of natural resources in the global south should first and foremost support development in that region, rather than enriching external actors. Ensuring that these rewards are shared equitably would help strengthen domestic finances and reduce dependency on external loans, which often come with restrictive or harmful conditions. A global financial transaction tax could play a central role in this effort, generating funds from cross-border financial trades and flows that could be reinvested in social infrastructure, global public goods such as health and water, and sustainable development initiatives. Finally, there must be protections in place to make all actors, public and private, answerable for outcomes and prevent further debt burdens from undermining countries’ development. Transparency is also essential to reveal hidden liabilities and fiscal risks that could destabilize economies. Together, these principles provide a road map for reform that is not only fair and effective but capable of fostering shared prosperity, resilience, and a more equitable global order. These ideas are not utopian. Several movements are already advancing them. The Bridgetown Initiative, launched by Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley in 2022, aims to redesign the international financial architecture to provide low- and middle-income countries with debt relief and affordable access to green finance. Its key policy proposals include expanding liquidity through the IMF by suspending surcharges and improving access to rapid-financing facilities, as well as redirecting at least $100 billion worth of unused Special Drawing Rights—international reserve assets created by the IMF to supplement countries’ official reserves—to low-income and climate-vulnerable nations. The initiative also calls for sovereign debt restructuring through the inclusion of natural disaster and pandemic clauses, scaling up concessional lending from multilateral development banks, and reforming global financial governance to amplify the voices of developing countries. For example, Barbados has already introduced a natural disaster clause in its sovereign bonds that pauses debt repayments for up to two years following a major disaster. It has also influenced major international discussions, leading to the establishment of the loss and damage fund at the 2022 U.N. Climate Change Conference and the 2023 Summit for a New Global Financing Pact in Paris, which produced the Pact for Prosperity, People, and the Planet. Similarly, efforts such as the Jubilee Commission, a Vatican-backed expert panel I belong to that aims to address the global sovereign debt and development crises, point to the growing recognition that the international financial system must evolve. Yet for these initiatives to succeed, they must form part of a more coherent and transformative strategy—one that gives global south countries genuine agency over their own development paths. High levels of public debt, for which the global financial system bears substantial responsibility, currently constrain this possibility. They confine the global south to narrow negotiations over the cost of capital or mechanisms such as loss and damage funds, instead of enabling them to participate in shaping a fairer and more sustainable international order. There are already signs that the global financial system as a whole is starting to reorient itself. The BRICS bloc—originally composed of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa and now including Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates—is set to play an increasingly influential role. Over the past two decades, BRICS has grown to represent more than a third of the global economy and half of the world’s population, and it aims to provide a counterbalance to Western dominance in international institutions. This shift is also evident in the growing emphasis on mission-oriented finance, although the term “missions” is often used without the institutional transformation needed to make them truly outcome driven. The World Bank’s Mission 300, which aims to provide electricity to 300 million people in Africa by 2030, combines public and private investment to expand power generation and transmission, scale up decentralized renewable solutions such as minigrids, and improve affordability and regional integration. It also emphasizes community empowerment, particularly for women, by enabling access to clean energy that fosters local enterprise. In many ways, Mission 300 aligns with several principles of the common-good compass. It promotes co-creation through collaboration with governments and local partners, supports collective learning via open data and shared platforms, and seeks fairer reward sharing by linking investment to social outcomes rather than short-term returns. It also emphasizes accountability and transparency through public reporting and feedback mechanisms, indicating a move toward more participatory governance. At the same time, the initiative highlights the need for a more rigorous and explicit framework grounded in the common good to ensure these elements are applied consistently and not left to chance. As organizations increasingly adopt “mission” or outcome-driven language, the real challenge lies in ensuring that they design and implement these missions effectively, with careful attention to the common good. The success of Mission 300 and similar initiatives will depend on practical details such as governance structures, accountability mechanisms, and sustained financing—factors that determine whether missions can deliver tangible and lasting change. What does this all mean for a world without rules? It means, first, refusing the false choice between the old order and no order. The rules we inherited were not neutral, and their unraveling is in part a crisis of their own making: Institutions that concentrated voice and rewards among the few could not indefinitely command the loyalty of the many. But it also means recognizing that the alternative to bad rules is not the law of the strongest—it is better rules, designed around the common good. This is also not a task for some distant constitutional moment. Every capital increase and replenishment round, every review of the capital adequacy framework, every debt restructuring, every new fund, from loss and damage to Mission 300, is an opportunity to embed the compass in institutional design. The questions that negotiators, ministers, and multilateral leaders should carry into every room are concrete: Does this instrument serve a clearly articulated mission, or does it merely move money? Who sat at the table when it was designed? Will the knowledge it generates be shared or enclosed? Who bears the risks, and who captures the rewards? And to whom, exactly, is this institution accountable? Bridgetown, the Jubilee Commission, natural disaster clauses in sovereign bonds—the seeds of a common-good architecture already exist. What they lack is not ambition but a coherent framework that connects them and holds every actor, from the IMF to the largest asset managers, answerable to outcomes. Surviving in a world without rules, in other words, does not depend on nostalgia, and it certainly does not depend on nationalism. It depends on our willingness to write the rules again—this time together and with the common good at the center. This is not utopian. Countries commit to goals of this kind every year in international forums. What has been missing is a systemic framework that holds them to account. The compass provides one. Now, we just need to use it. Mariana Mazzucato is a professor in the economics of innovation and public value at University College London (UCL), where she is the founding director of the UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose. She is the author of Mission Economy: A Moonshot Guide to Changing Capitalism and the forthcoming The Common Good Economy: A New Compass. She served as a special advisor to President Cyril Ramaphosa for South Africa’s G-20 presidency and advises governments, including Brazil and Spain, on mission-oriented industrial strategy. item.title: AI Is Changing the Rules of Entrepreneurship
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.65
Summary. Today, a single individual enabled by AI can—at very low cost—perform many activities needed to establish a startup quickly and in parallel: generating product ideas, simulating Almost two decades ago, the entrepreneur and author Eric Ries launched a methodology for the “lean startup.” In this approach, a new business could be launched with just capital, a minimum viable product, a team, extensive discussions with potential customers, and a process of repeated pivoting as the startup scaled. The lean startup approach combined Toyota’s lean manufacturing method with Stanford professor Steve Blank’s approaches to customer development. Because founders typically had few resources at their disposal, the lean approach took hold.

item.title: Research: How Curveball Questions Can Surface the Insight You’re Looking For
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.38
Research: How Curveball Questions Can Surface the Insight You’re Looking For Summary. Traditional “tough” questions often elicit polished talking points rather than candid answers. A more revealing approach is the curveball: a question that is closely tied to what We’re all taught to ask tough questions. Interviewers are coached to use open-ended prompts to get beyond rehearsed answers. Managers press for specifics when employees speak in generalities. Journalists and negotiators follow up when someone evades the point. The aim is the same: to uncover information the other person may be reluctant to reveal.

item.title: You Need to Understand Your Employees’ Caregiving Responsibilities
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.84
You Need to Understand Your Employees’ Caregiving Responsibilities Summary. Employees regularly balance work with caregiving responsibilities, whether it is child care, eldercare, or caring for another family member. Yet many organizations lack visibility into who their Most of us are caregivers. Seventy-three percent of all U.S. employees, and 71% of employees globally, identify as caregivers with responsibilities to look after children, aging parents, or other family members. Fifty-four percent of employees in their 40s identify as sandwiched caregivers, providing for the needs of parents aged 65 and older while also raising children or providing for a young adult child 18 years and older.
